Adam Adam was the first man, made by God from the dust of the ground and placed in the garden of Eden. Who. Adam’s name is the ordinary Hebrew word for “man” or “mankind”, and it sounds like the word for “ground”. He was created on the sixth day of creation, in the image of God, as the head of the whole human race. Eve was his wife; Cain, Abel and Seth were among his sons. He lived 930 years. Their story. God formed Adam, breathed life into him and gave him work and a single command in the garden (Genesis 2). Adam listened to his wife rather than to God and ate the forbidden fruit, and sin and death entered the world (Genesis 3). God clothed him and sent him out of Eden, yet promised a Saviour born of the woman (Genesis 3:15; 5:1–5). Remember. Adam acted for all of us, and in him all die. Paul calls Christ “the last Adam”: where the first Adam disobeyed in a garden, Christ obeyed to the point of death, and everyone joined to him by faith is made alive (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45). Genesis 2:7 then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature. Adam was made directly by God, body and soul, not by chance. Romans 5:12 Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned One man’s sin brought death to the whole human race. 1 Corinthians 15:22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. Adam and Christ are the two heads of humanity: one brings death, the other life. Every human story runs back to Adam, and every hope runs forward to the last Adam, Jesus Christ.

Eve Eve was the first woman, created from Adam’s side as his wife and called “the mother of all living”. Who. Eve was made by God on the sixth day, from a rib taken from Adam, to be his helper and companion, equal in dignity and made in God’s image. Her name sounds like the Hebrew word for “life”. She was the mother of Cain, Abel and Seth. Their story. God brought Eve to Adam, and the first marriage began with joy (Genesis 2:18–25). The serpent deceived her into doubting God’s word; she ate the fruit and gave some to her husband (Genesis 3:1–6). God judged her with pain in childbearing and conflict in marriage, yet promised that her offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15–16). After Abel’s murder she bore Seth and saw God’s mercy continue (Genesis 4:1, 25). Remember. Eve’s fall is a warning against listening to any voice that questions what God has said (2 Corinthians 11:3). But her story does not end in judgment. The promise made to her is the first gospel promise in the Bible, fulfilled when Christ, born of a woman, defeated the devil (Galatians 4:4). Genesis 2:22 And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man. Eve was God’s own gift to Adam, made from him and for him. Genesis 3:15 I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel. Even in the curse God promised a son of Eve who would defeat the serpent. Genesis 3:20 The man called his wife’s name Eve, because she was the mother of all living. Adam named her in faith that life would go on despite the sentence of death.

Cain Cain was Adam and Eve’s firstborn son, who murdered his brother Abel. Who. Cain was the first child born in the Bible, a farmer who worked the ground. Do not confuse him with Kenan, a descendant of Seth with a similar name (Genesis 5:9). His son Enoch is also different from the godly Enoch who walked with God. Their story. Cain brought an offering of crops, but God did not accept it, because Cain’s heart and life were not right (Genesis 4:3–7; Hebrews 11:4). God warned him that sin was crouching at the door, but Cain, angry and jealous, killed Abel in the field. When God asked where his brother was, he answered, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:8–9). God sent him away as a wanderer but put a mark on him to protect him. He settled in the land of Nod and built a city, and his family became known for skill and for violence (Genesis 4:10–24). Remember. Cain shows how quickly sin grows from envy to murder, and how religion without faith is empty (1 John 3:12). Yet even Cain received a mark of protection: God restrains evil and is patient with sinners. Genesis 4:7 If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it. God warned Cain kindly before he sinned. Genesis 4:8 Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him. The first death in the Bible is a murder within a family. 1 John 3:12 We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous. John makes Cain the pattern of hatred towards the righteous.

Abel Abel was Adam and Eve’s second son, a shepherd whose offering God accepted and who was murdered by his brother Cain. Who. Abel was the younger brother of Cain and a keeper of sheep. His name in Hebrew means “breath” or “vapour”, a fitting name for a life cut short. Jesus calls him “righteous Abel”, the first of the martyrs (Matthew 23:35). Their story. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions as an offering, and God accepted him and his gift (Genesis 4:2–4). The difference was faith: Abel trusted God and offered his best (Hebrews 11:4). His brother Cain, jealous of God’s favour, killed him in the field. Abel’s blood cried out to God from the ground (Genesis 4:8–10). Seth was later born in his place (Genesis 4:25). Remember. Abel teaches that God looks at the heart and receives those who come to him by faith. His blood cried for justice; the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word”, because it brings forgiveness and peace with God (Hebrews 12:24). Hebrews 11:4 By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. Abel’s offering was accepted because it came from faith. Hebrews 12:24 and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. Christ’s blood speaks mercy where Abel’s called for justice.

Seth Seth was the third named son of Adam and Eve, born after Abel’s death, through whom the godly line continued. Who. Seth was born when Adam was 130 years old. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for “appointed”, because Eve said God had appointed another child in place of Abel. He lived 912 years. His son was Enosh. Their story. Seth’s birth gave Adam and Eve a new beginning after the murder of Abel (Genesis 4:25). In his son’s day “people began to call upon the name of the LORD”, the first mention of public worship (Genesis 4:26). Genesis 5 traces the family line from Adam through Seth to Noah, a line marked by ordinary lives, each ending with “and he died”, until Enoch walked with God. Luke’s genealogy runs from Jesus back through Seth to Adam (Luke 3:38). Remember. Seth reminds us that God does not let sin and death have the last word. When the line of promise seemed broken, God gave another son, and kept the family going that would one day lead to Christ. Genesis 4:25 And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, “God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.” Eve saw Seth as God’s gift to carry on the promise. Genesis 4:26 To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD. In Seth’s family the worship of the true God took root. Luke 3:38 the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God. Jesus’ family line runs back through Seth.

Enoch Enoch was a godly man from the line of Seth who walked with God and was taken to heaven without dying. Who. Enoch was the son of Jared and the father of Methuselah, “the seventh from Adam” (Jude 14). He is different from Enoch the son of Cain, after whom Cain named a city (Genesis 4:17). Their story. Genesis tells Enoch’s life in a few lines. After Methuselah was born he “walked with God” for three hundred years, living in close daily fellowship with him in a corrupt age. After 365 years “he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:21–24). Hebrews says he was taken up so that he did not see death, because he pleased God by faith (Hebrews 11:5). Jude says he warned his generation that the Lord would come in judgment with his holy ones (Jude 14–15). Remember. Enoch’s story shines in the long list of “and he died”. It shows that walking with God by faith is possible in an ungodly world, and it gives a glimpse of the victory over death that Christ secures for all his people. Genesis 5:24 Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. A whole life summed up as fellowship with God. Hebrews 11:5 By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God. Enoch pleased God by faith, and God spared him death.

Methuselah Methuselah was the son of Enoch and grandfather of Noah, the longest-lived person recorded in the Bible. Who. Methuselah was the son of the godly Enoch and the father of Lamech, who was Noah’s father. He belongs to Seth’s line, and he is not the same person as Methushael in Cain’s line (Genesis 4:18). Their story. Almost all the Bible says about Methuselah is in Genesis 5:21–27. He fathered Lamech at 187 years old, had other sons and daughters, and died at 969, the greatest age the Bible records. If you add up the ages in Genesis 5 and 7, he seems to have died in the very year of the flood, though Scripture does not say whether before it or in it (Genesis 5:25–27; 7:6). Some have suggested his name hints at coming judgment, but the meaning is uncertain. Remember. Even the longest human life ends: “and he died”. Methuselah’s years also show God’s patience, waiting long before he sent the flood (1 Peter 3:20). Our hope is not in a long life but in the eternal life Christ gives. Genesis 5:27 Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died. The longest life in Scripture still ended in death, the result of sin.

Noah Noah was the righteous man whom God saved with his family through the flood in the ark. Who. Noah was the son of Lamech in the line of Seth, and the grandson of Methuselah. His three sons were Shem, Ham and Japheth. He was 600 years old when the flood came and lived 950 years in all. Their story. When the earth was filled with violence, God resolved to judge it, “but Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8). God told him to build an ark, and Noah did all that God commanded (Genesis 6:9–22). He and seven others were saved when the flood covered the earth (Genesis 7–8). Afterwards he offered sacrifice, and God made a covenant never again to destroy the earth by flood, with the rainbow as its sign (Genesis 8:20–9:17). Later Noah planted a vineyard, became drunk and was shamed in his tent (Genesis 9:20–27). Remember. Noah was saved by grace through faith, not by his own goodness, and he too fell into sin. The ark is a picture of Christ: all who are in him are safe from judgment (1 Peter 3:20–21). Jesus says his return will come as suddenly as the flood (Matthew 24:37). Genesis 6:8 But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD. Noah’s rescue began with God’s grace. Hebrews 11:7 By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. His faith showed itself in years of obedient work. Genesis 9:13 I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. God’s covenant with Noah still upholds the world today.

Shem, Ham and Japheth Shem, Ham and Japheth were the three sons of Noah, saved with him in the ark, from whom all the nations descend. Who. They were Noah’s sons, born before the flood, each with his wife on the ark. Genesis 10, sometimes called the Table of Nations, traces the peoples of the world from them. Broadly, Shem’s descendants include the Hebrews and other peoples of the Near East (the word “Semite” comes from Shem); Ham’s include Egypt, Cush and Canaan; Japheth’s include peoples to the north and west. Their story. After the flood Noah became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Ham saw his father’s nakedness and told his brothers; Shem and Japheth covered him respectfully. Noah then cursed Ham’s son Canaan and blessed Shem and Japheth (Genesis 9:20–27). Shem’s line leads to Abraham (Genesis 11:10–26) and appears in Jesus’ genealogy (Luke 3:36). Remember. The curse fell on Canaan, not on any race, and it has wrongly been used to justify slavery. All people come from one family (Acts 17:26). God chose Shem’s line to bring the Saviour, so that blessing would reach every nation, including Japheth’s and Ham’s. Genesis 10:1 These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The whole world was repopulated from these three brothers. Genesis 9:26 He also said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. The LORD is named as Shem’s God, pointing to the line of promise.

Abraham Abraham was the father of the Israelite nation, called by God to leave his homeland and trust his promises. Who. Abraham (first called Abram) lived about 2000 BC. He came from Ur in Mesopotamia and was the son of Terah, a descendant of Shem. His wife was Sarah; his sons were Ishmael (by Hagar) and Isaac. He lived 175 years. Their story. At 75 God called him to go to a land he would show him, promising him a great name, many descendants and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–4). He rescued his nephew Lot and was blessed by Melchizedek (Genesis 14). He believed God’s promise, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). God made a covenant with him, sealed by circumcision, and renamed him Abraham, “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17). Isaac was born when he was 100 (Genesis 21). He was willing to offer Isaac on Mount Moriah, and God provided a ram instead (Genesis 22). Remember. Abraham was no flawless hero: twice he lied that Sarah was his sister, and he took Hagar to hurry God’s promise (Genesis 12; 16; 20). He was justified by faith, not works, and all who believe in Christ are his children (Romans 4; Galatians 3:7–9). Genesis 12:3 I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. God’s plan for Abraham was always for the whole world. Genesis 15:6 And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness. The key verse for justification by faith alone. Galatians 3:8 And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” Paul calls God’s promise to Abraham the gospel preached in advance. Abraham’s faith shows that God saves sinners who simply trust his promise, fulfilled in Christ, Abraham’s offspring.

Sarah Sarah was Abraham’s wife and the mother of Isaac, the son God promised. Who. Sarah (first called Sarai) was Abraham’s wife and also his half-sister, the daughter of his father by another mother (Genesis 20:12). She was beautiful, and she was barren for most of her life. God renamed her Sarah, meaning “princess”. She died aged 127 and was buried at Machpelah near Hebron. Their story. She left Ur and Haran with Abraham and twice was taken into a king’s household when Abraham called her his sister (Genesis 12; 20). Unable to have children, she gave her servant Hagar to Abraham, then treated Hagar harshly (Genesis 16). When the LORD promised her a son in her old age, she laughed in disbelief (Genesis 18:10–15). God kept his word: at 90 she bore Isaac, and her laughter turned to joy (Genesis 21:1–7). Remember. Sarah’s story is about God doing what is impossible. Her impatience and unbelief did not cancel his promise. Hebrews counts her among the faithful, and Peter holds her up as an example of trusting, unafraid hope in God (Hebrews 11:11; 1 Peter 3:5–6). Genesis 18:14 Is anything too hard for the LORD? God answered Sarah’s laughter with a question that still strengthens faith. Genesis 21:1 The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. God kept his promise exactly. Hebrews 11:11 By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. In the end Sarah trusted the God who promised.

Hagar Hagar was Sarah’s Egyptian servant who bore Abraham his son Ishmael. Who. Hagar was an Egyptian slave woman in Sarah’s household, probably acquired during Abraham’s time in Egypt. She became the mother of Ishmael. Their story. When Sarah could not have children she gave Hagar to Abraham as a second wife. Hagar conceived and looked down on Sarah, and Sarah treated her so harshly that she ran away. In the wilderness the angel of the LORD found her, sent her back and promised her many descendants. She named the LORD “a God of seeing” (Genesis 16). After Isaac was born, Sarah demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. When their water ran out in the wilderness of Beersheba, God heard the boy crying, showed Hagar a well and promised to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 21:8–21). Paul later uses Hagar as a picture of slavery under the law (Galatians 4:21–31). Remember. Hagar was used and mistreated by the family of promise, yet the God of Abraham saw her, heard her and cared for her. He is the God who sees the overlooked. Genesis 16:13 So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, “You are a God of seeing,” for she said, “Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.” An outcast servant is the first person in the Bible to give God a name. Genesis 21:17 And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, “What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. God heard and helped when Hagar had given up hope.

Ishmael Ishmael was Abraham’s first son, born to Hagar the Egyptian servant. Who. Ishmael was born when Abraham was 86, about fourteen years before Isaac. His name means “God hears”. He became the father of twelve tribal chiefs in the deserts south and east of Canaan, and lived 137 years. Esau married one of his daughters. Their story. The angel told Hagar before his birth that he would be “a wild donkey of a man”, at odds with others (Genesis 16:11–12). Abraham hoped Ishmael would be his heir, but God said the covenant would be with Isaac, though he would bless Ishmael too (Genesis 17:18–21). He was circumcised at 13. At Isaac’s weaning feast Ishmael mocked his brother, and he and his mother were sent away; God cared for them in the wilderness (Genesis 21:8–21). Ishmael and Isaac together buried their father (Genesis 25:9). Remember. Ishmael was blessed, but he was not the child of promise. Paul uses him to show the difference between relying on human effort and relying on God’s promise (Galatians 4:22–31). God’s saving purposes are by grace, not by natural birth. Genesis 17:20 As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. God answered Abraham’s prayer for Ishmael with real blessing. Genesis 21:12 through Isaac shall your offspring be named. The line of promise ran through Isaac, not Ishmael.

Lot Lot was Abraham’s nephew who settled in Sodom and was rescued when God destroyed the city. Who. Lot was the son of Haran, Abraham’s brother who died in Ur. He travelled with Abraham from Haran to Canaan. His two daughters became the ancestors of the Moabites and the Ammonites. Their story. When their flocks grew too large, Abraham let Lot choose first, and Lot chose the well-watered Jordan valley, moving his tent towards Sodom, whose people were very wicked (Genesis 13). He was taken captive in a war and rescued by Abraham (Genesis 14). Later he lived in Sodom and sat in its gate. When two angels came, he protected them but offered his daughters to the mob. The angels dragged the reluctant Lot and his family out before the city was destroyed; his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:1–26). His daughters then made him drunk and had children by him (Genesis 19:30–38). Remember. Lot was “righteous” and troubled by the evil around him, yet he drifted towards the world and nearly lost everything (2 Peter 2:7–8). He was saved only because the LORD was merciful to him. Genesis 19:16 But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. Lot’s rescue was pure mercy; even then he hesitated. 2 Peter 2:7 and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked Peter counts Lot among the righteous, a believer who was compromised. Luke 17:32 Remember Lot’s wife. Jesus warns against looking back to the world when judgment comes.

Melchizedek Melchizedek was the king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abraham. Who. Melchizedek appears suddenly in Genesis 14 as king of Salem (probably the early name of Jerusalem) and “priest of God Most High”, long before the priesthood of Aaron. His name means “king of righteousness”, and Salem means “peace”. Some have tried to identify him with Shem or with an appearance of Christ, but Scripture presents him as a real king and priest, whose origins it does not record. Their story. Abraham was returning from rescuing Lot when Melchizedek brought out bread and wine, blessed him in the name of God Most High, and received from him a tenth of everything (Genesis 14:17–20). Centuries later David wrote that the coming Lord would be “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews explains that Melchizedek, with no recorded genealogy, birth or death, resembles the Son of God, and that his priesthood is greater than Levi’s (Hebrews 7:1–17). Remember. Melchizedek points to Christ, our King and Priest in one person: righteous, bringing peace, and living forever to intercede for us. Genesis 14:18 And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.) A king and priest of the true God outside Abraham’s family. Psalm 110:4 The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.” God promised the Messiah a priesthood of Melchizedek’s kind. Hebrews 7:3 He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever. Scripture’s silence about his origins makes him a picture of the eternal Son.

Isaac Isaac was the son God promised to Abraham and Sarah, and the father of Esau and Jacob. Who. Isaac was born when Abraham was 100 and Sarah 90. His name means “he laughs”, recalling his parents’ laughter at God’s promise. He married Rebekah at 40 and became the father of twins at 60. He lived 180 years and was buried at Machpelah. Their story. As a young man he carried the wood up Mount Moriah, where his father was ready to sacrifice him until God provided a ram (Genesis 22). Abraham’s servant found Rebekah for him, and he loved her (Genesis 24). God renewed to him the promises made to Abraham (Genesis 26:2–5). Like his father he lied that his wife was his sister (Genesis 26:6–11). He favoured Esau, and in his old age and blindness he was deceived into giving the blessing to Jacob (Genesis 25:28; 27). Remember. Isaac was a quieter man than his father or his son, and his favouritism caused real harm. Yet he was the child of promise, born by God’s power. On Moriah he pictures the only Son whom the Father did not spare (Hebrews 11:17–19; Romans 8:32). Genesis 22:2 Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering The test of Moriah foreshadows the Father giving his only Son. Genesis 22:8 Abraham said, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” Isaac was spared because God provided a substitute. Genesis 26:3 Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. God’s covenant passed on to Isaac.

Rebekah Rebekah was Isaac’s wife and the mother of the twins Esau and Jacob. Who. Rebekah was the daughter of Bethuel and the sister of Laban, from Abraham’s relatives in Haran in northern Mesopotamia. She was buried at Machpelah with Isaac. Their story. Abraham’s servant prayed for a sign, and Rebekah answered it by kindly watering his camels. She agreed to leave her family and go to marry a man she had never met, and Isaac loved her (Genesis 24). She was barren for twenty years until Isaac prayed. When the twins struggled in her womb, the LORD told her “the older shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:21–26). She loved Jacob more than Esau, and when Isaac planned to bless Esau, she arranged for Jacob to deceive his blind father and take the blessing. She then had to send Jacob away to Laban, and as far as Scripture records she never saw him again (Genesis 27). Remember. Rebekah began with bold faith but later tried to secure God’s promise by deceit, and her family paid a heavy price. God’s purpose for Jacob stood by his own choosing, not by her scheming (Romans 9:10–13). Genesis 24:67 Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. God’s guidance led to a loving marriage. Genesis 25:23 And the LORD said to her, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger.” God revealed his choice of Jacob before the twins were born.

Esau Esau was Isaac’s elder twin son, who sold his birthright to Jacob and became the ancestor of the Edomites. Who. Esau was born first, red and hairy, and became a skilful hunter, his father’s favourite. He was also called Edom (“red”), and his descendants, the Edomites, lived in the hill country of Seir, south-east of the Dead Sea. He married two Hittite women, to his parents’ grief, and later a daughter of Ishmael. Their story. Coming home hungry, Esau sold his birthright, the firstborn’s double share and headship, to Jacob for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25:29–34). When Jacob tricked Isaac into giving him the blessing, Esau wept bitterly and planned to kill him (Genesis 27). Twenty years later he ran to meet the returning Jacob and embraced him (Genesis 33:4). The two buried their father together (Genesis 35:29). Edom and Israel remained in conflict for centuries (Obadiah). Remember. Esau was generous in the end, but Hebrews calls him “unholy” because he traded God’s blessing for a moment’s appetite (Hebrews 12:16–17). God’s choice of Jacob over Esau shows that salvation rests on his mercy, not human merit (Romans 9:10–16). Genesis 25:34 Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright. Esau valued an instant meal over God’s promise. Hebrews 12:16 that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. Esau is a warning against despising spiritual things. Genesis 33:4 But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept. God softened Esau’s anger and brought reconciliation.

Jacob (Israel) Jacob, renamed Israel, was Isaac’s younger twin son and the father of the twelve tribes of Israel. Who. Jacob was the son of Isaac and Rebekah and the twin of Esau. His name sounds like “heel” and came to mean “deceiver”, because he was born holding his brother’s heel. God renamed him Israel. He married Leah and Rachel, and had twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah. He died in Egypt aged 147. Their story. Jacob bought Esau’s birthright and deceived his father to take the blessing (Genesis 25; 27). Fleeing from Esau, he dreamed at Bethel of a ladder to heaven, and God repeated Abraham’s promises to him (Genesis 28). His uncle Laban deceived him in turn, and he served twenty years for his wives and flocks (Genesis 29–31). Returning home, he wrestled through the night with God at Peniel and was renamed Israel (Genesis 32). His favouritism towards Joseph tore the family apart, but he was reunited with Joseph in Egypt and blessed his sons before he died (Genesis 37–49). Remember. Jacob was a grasping schemer, yet God chose him, kept him and changed him. The whole people of God bears his new name. Jesus said he is the true ladder joining heaven and earth (John 1:51). Genesis 28:15 Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you. God made promises to Jacob when he deserved nothing. Genesis 32:28 Then he said, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.” At Peniel God broke and blessed Jacob and gave him a new name. Hosea 12:4 He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. Jacob prevailed by clinging to God in weakness and tears.

Leah Leah was Jacob’s first wife, the elder daughter of Laban and mother of six of the twelve tribes. Who. Leah was Laban’s elder daughter and Rachel’s sister. Genesis says her eyes were “weak”, perhaps meaning dull or tender, while Rachel was beautiful. She bore Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and a daughter, Dinah. She was buried at Machpelah beside Abraham, Isaac and their wives. Their story. Laban tricked Jacob by giving him Leah on the wedding night instead of Rachel (Genesis 29:21–26). Jacob loved Rachel more, but the LORD saw that Leah was unloved and gave her children. The names she chose trace her heart: she hoped her husband would love her, until at Judah’s birth she said, “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:31–35). She was caught up in a bitter rivalry with Rachel and gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob (Genesis 30). Remember. Leah was the unwanted wife, yet God chose her as the mother of Levi, the priestly tribe, and Judah, the royal tribe from which David and Jesus came. God sees the unloved and builds his kingdom through them. Genesis 29:31 When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. God noticed and honoured the unloved wife. Genesis 29:35 And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she called his name Judah. Leah turned from longing for Jacob’s love to praising God. Ruth 4:11 May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. Israel remembered both sisters as mothers of the nation.

Rachel Rachel was Jacob’s beloved wife, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin. Who. Rachel was the younger daughter of Laban and sister of Leah. She was a shepherdess, and Jacob loved her from their first meeting at the well. She was barren for many years, then bore Joseph and later Benjamin. She died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried on the road to Bethlehem. Their story. Jacob served seven years for her, and then, after Laban’s trick, another seven (Genesis 29). Envious of her sister’s children, she cried, “Give me children, or I shall die!” and gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob (Genesis 30:1–8). At last God remembered her, and Joseph was born (Genesis 30:22–24). When the family left Laban, she stole her father’s household idols and hid them by deceit (Genesis 31:19, 34–35). She died near Bethlehem, naming her son Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow” (Genesis 35:16–20). Remember. Rachel was deeply loved but often unhappy, envious and grasping. Jeremiah pictures her weeping for her exiled children, and Matthew hears that weeping at Herod’s slaughter in Bethlehem, where the Saviour who wipes away every tear had just been born (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:18). Genesis 29:20 So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her. A rare picture of romantic love in Genesis. Genesis 30:22 Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb. Children came as God’s answer, not by Rachel’s schemes. Jeremiah 31:15 Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more. Rachel became a symbol of Israel’s grief, answered in Christ.

The twelve sons of Jacob The twelve sons of Jacob were the fathers of the twelve tribes of Israel. Who. By Leah: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. By Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. By Rachel’s servant Bilhah: Dan and Naphtali. By Leah’s servant Zilpah: Gad and Asher. Later Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each became a tribe, while Levi’s tribe received no territory but served as priests and temple workers. Their story. The brothers were all born in about twenty years, most in Haran (Genesis 29–30; 35:16–18). Their story is full of sin: Simeon and Levi massacred the men of Shechem (Genesis 34), Reuben slept with his father’s concubine (Genesis 35:22), and the brothers sold Joseph into slavery (Genesis 37). Through famine and Joseph’s testing God brought them to repentance and reunited them in Egypt (Genesis 42–45). Jacob’s dying words to each son foretold the future of his tribe (Genesis 49). Remember. God built his people from twelve troubled, jealous men, not from heroes. Jesus chose twelve apostles to show he was renewing Israel, and the new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates (Revelation 21:12). Genesis 49:28 All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him. The twelve sons became the twelve tribes. Acts 7:8 and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. Stephen calls them the patriarchs of the nation. Revelation 21:12 on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed The twelve tribes are remembered in the eternal city.

Joseph Joseph was Jacob’s favourite son, sold into slavery by his brothers, who rose to rule Egypt and saved his family from famine. Who. Joseph was the elder son of Rachel and the eleventh of Jacob’s twelve sons. Do not confuse him with Joseph the husband of Mary, or Joseph of Arimathea. He married Asenath in Egypt and had two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. He died aged 110. Their story. Jacob gave him a special robe, and his dreams of ruling his brothers made them hate him; they sold him to traders bound for Egypt (Genesis 37). He served Potiphar faithfully, refused his master’s wife, and was falsely imprisoned (Genesis 39). God enabled him to interpret dreams, and at 30 Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt to prepare for seven years of famine (Genesis 40–41). When his brothers came to buy grain, he tested them, then revealed himself and forgave them (Genesis 42–45). He brought Jacob’s family to live in Egypt (Genesis 46–47). Remember. As a young man Joseph was proud and tactless. His great lesson is God’s providence: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Like Joseph, Jesus was rejected by his brothers, then raised to the throne to save many. Genesis 39:2 The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. God was with Joseph even as a slave. Genesis 45:5 for God sent me before you to preserve life. Joseph saw God’s hand behind his brothers’ sin. Genesis 50:20 As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. God rules even over human evil for the good of his people.

Judah Judah was the fourth son of Jacob and Leah, the ancestor of the royal tribe of David and Jesus. Who. Judah was born to Leah, who named him from the word for “praise”. His tribe became the largest in Israel and later gave its name to the southern kingdom and to the Jews. He had sons by a Canaanite wife, and twins, Perez and Zerah, by Tamar. Do not confuse him with other men called Judah or Judas in the Bible. Their story. It was Judah who proposed selling Joseph to traders rather than killing him (Genesis 37:26–27). He then left his brothers, married a Canaanite, and wronged his daughter-in-law Tamar, until he confessed, “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38). Later he pledged himself for Benjamin’s safety and offered to become a slave in Benjamin’s place, a turning point that moved Joseph to reveal himself (Genesis 43:8–9; 44:18–34). Jacob foretold that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:8–12). Remember. Judah shows real repentance: the man who sold one brother was ready to give himself for another. From him came David and finally Jesus, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, who gave himself for us (Revelation 5:5). Genesis 44:33 Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers. The changed Judah offered himself as a substitute. Genesis 49:10 The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples. Jacob promised lasting kingship to Judah’s line. Revelation 5:5 behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered Christ is the King from Judah’s tribe.

Tamar (Genesis 38) Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah, who bore him twin sons and became an ancestor of David and Jesus. Who. This Tamar is the wife of Judah’s sons Er and Onan, in Genesis 38. She is different from David’s daughter Tamar (2 Samuel 13) and Absalom’s daughter (2 Samuel 14:27). She was probably a Canaanite. Her sons were Perez and Zerah. Their story. Tamar married Judah’s eldest son Er, whom the LORD put to death for his wickedness. By custom the next brother, Onan, was to give her a child in his brother’s name, but he refused, and he also died. Judah promised her his youngest son Shelah, but never kept his word (Genesis 38:6–11). Years later Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute by the road, and Judah, not recognising her, slept with her and left his seal, cord and staff as a pledge. When she was found pregnant he ordered her burned, until she produced his pledge. Judah confessed, “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:12–26). She bore twins, Perez and Zerah. Remember. This is a sordid story of sin on both sides, yet God wove it into his saving plan. Tamar is one of the women named in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:3), a sign of the grace that came to save sinners. Genesis 38:26 Then Judah identified them and said, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” Judah admitted that his own sin had driven Tamar to act. Matthew 1:3 and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar Matthew deliberately names Tamar in the Messiah’s family line.

Job Job was a righteous man from the land of Uz whose terrible sufferings and restoration are told in the book of Job. Who. Job lived in Uz, probably in the region of Edom or northern Arabia. When he lived is uncertain, but his wealth in flocks, his offering of sacrifices for his family and his long life suggest the time of the patriarchs. He was not an Israelite, but he feared the true God. He had seven sons and three daughters. Their story. God allowed Satan to test Job, and in one day he lost his flocks, servants and children, then his health (Job 1–2). Yet he worshipped and did not curse God. His three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, insisted he must be suffering for some secret sin. Job protested his innocence and longed to meet God, sometimes speaking rashly (Job 3–31). A younger man, Elihu, spoke next (Job 32–37). Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, showing his wisdom and power in creation. Job repented and was humbled, and God rebuked the friends and restored Job’s fortunes twice over (Job 38–42). Remember. Not all suffering is punishment for a particular sin, and God is good and wise even when he does not explain himself. Job’s cry, “I know that my Redeemer lives”, finds its answer in Christ (Job 19:25; James 5:11). Job 1:21 Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. Job worshipped God in the hour of his greatest loss. Job 19:25 For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth. In his darkness Job held on to a living Redeemer. James 5:11 You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful. Job’s story ends by revealing God’s mercy.

Moses The prophet through whom God led Israel out of Egypt and gave his law at Mount Sinai. Who. Moses was born in Egypt, probably about 1525 BC, to Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi; Aaron and Miriam were his elder brother and sister. He lived 120 years: forty in Egypt, forty as a shepherd in Midian, and forty leading Israel. He married Jethro’s daughter Zipporah. Their story. Hidden on the Nile as a baby, he was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter; later he killed an Egyptian and fled to Midian (Exodus 2). God called him at the burning bush and revealed his name, I AM (Exodus 3–4). Through the plagues and the Passover God brought Israel out and through the Red Sea (Exodus 5–15). At Sinai Moses received the law (Exodus 19–40), then led the people through the wilderness (Numbers). Because he struck the rock in anger instead of speaking to it, he was not allowed to enter Canaan (Numbers 20:1–13). He died on Mount Nebo, looking over it (Deuteronomy 34). Remember. Moses was very humble (Numbers 12:3), yet a sinner who killed a man and dishonoured God before the people. He foretold a greater prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15). That prophet is Christ, faithful over God’s house as a Son, where Moses was faithful as a servant (Hebrews 3:5–6). The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Deuteronomy 34:10 And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, No other Old Testament prophet knew God so closely, which is why the coming of a prophet greater than Moses was such news. Hebrews 11:24-26 By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward. Moses gave up the riches of Egypt by faith, looking ahead to God’s reward and sharing in advance the shame of Christ.

Aaron Moses’ elder brother and spokesman, and the first high priest of Israel. Who. Aaron, of the tribe of Levi, was three years older than Moses (Exodus 7:7). He married Elisheba, and his four sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. God gave the priesthood to him and his descendants, so every later priest in Israel, including Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, traced his line to Aaron. Their story. God sent him to speak for Moses before Pharaoh (Exodus 4:14–16; 7:1–2). With Hur he held up Moses’ hands during the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17:12). He was ordained high priest, with special garments, to offer sacrifices for the people (Exodus 28–29; Leviticus 8–9). Yet while Moses was on the mountain he made the golden calf, and then blamed the people (Exodus 32). Two of his sons died for offering fire the Lord had not commanded (Leviticus 10). With Miriam he grumbled against Moses (Numbers 12). His staff that budded confirmed God’s choice of him (Numbers 17). He died on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar succeeded him (Numbers 20:22–29). Remember. Aaron was a weak and sinful man who had to offer sacrifice for his own sins before the people’s. He points to the great high priest Jesus, who is sinless, lives for ever, and offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:23–28). Hebrews 5:4 And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was. Aaron did not appoint himself; God called him, just as God appointed Christ as high priest. Exodus 32:24 So I said to them, ‘Let any who have gold take it off.’ So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf. Aaron’s feeble excuse for the golden calf shows how even Israel’s high priest needed forgiveness.

Miriam The sister of Moses and Aaron, a prophetess who led Israel’s women in praise at the Red Sea. Who. Miriam was the daughter of Amram and Jochebed and the sister of Aaron and Moses (Numbers 26:59). Her name in Greek form is Mary, but she is not to be confused with any of the Marys of the New Testament. Their story. She is probably the sister who watched over baby Moses in the basket and offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse, who was their own mother (Exodus 2:4–8). After the crossing of the Red Sea she took a tambourine and led the women in song and dance (Exodus 15:20–21). Later she and Aaron spoke against Moses, partly over his Cushite wife and partly from jealousy of his authority. God struck her with a skin disease; Moses prayed for her, and after seven days shut outside the camp she was restored (Numbers 12). She died at Kadesh (Numbers 20:1). The prophet Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as leaders God sent to Israel (Micah 6:4). Remember. Miriam was gifted and used by God, yet envy brought her low. The God who disciplined her also healed her in answer to Moses’ prayer, a picture of the greater Mediator, Christ, who prays for his people. Exodus 15:20-21 Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing. And Miriam sang to them: “Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.” Miriam led Israel’s first great song of praise after God’s rescue at the Red Sea. Numbers 12:1-2 Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married, for he had married a Cushite woman. And they said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?” And the LORD heard it. Her complaint was really about position and honour, and God heard it.

Pharaoh of the exodus The unnamed king of Egypt who hardened his heart against God and would not let Israel go. Who. The Bible does not name him, and scholars differ on who he was. If the exodus took place about 1446 BC, as 1 Kings 6:1 suggests, he may have been Amenhotep II; others favour Rameses II and a later date. He may have been the successor of the king who first enslaved Israel (Exodus 1:8; 2:23). For the title and the other pharaohs of Scripture, see the Pharaoh card in The Bible’s World. Their story. When Moses asked him to let Israel go, he refused and made their slavery harder (Exodus 5). God sent ten plagues; several times Pharaoh promised to release the people and then went back on his word (Exodus 7–11). Scripture says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that the Lord hardened it. After the death of the firstborn he let the people go (Exodus 12:29–32), then changed his mind and pursued them, and his army was drowned in the Red Sea (Exodus 14). Remember. Pharaoh shows the folly of a proud heart that will not bow to God. Yet even his rebellion served God’s purpose to make his name known in all the earth (Romans 9:17). From his grip God redeemed his people by the blood of the Passover lamb, a picture of Christ, our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7). Exodus 5:2 But Pharaoh said, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.” Pharaoh’s first answer sets the theme of the plagues: he would come to know who the Lord is. Romans 9:17 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” Paul uses Pharaoh to show that God rules even over those who resist him.

Jethro The priest of Midian who was Moses’ father-in-law and gave him wise advice. Who. Jethro was a priest in Midian, the land east of Egypt where Moses fled. He is also called Reuel (Exodus 2:18), probably a second name or a family name; Numbers 10:29 mentions Hobab son of Reuel, and scholars differ on how these names fit together. His daughter Zipporah became Moses’ wife. Their story. Moses kept Jethro’s flocks for about forty years, and it was while tending them that he met God at the burning bush (Exodus 3:1). When Moses returned to Egypt, Jethro sent him off in peace (Exodus 4:18). After the exodus Jethro brought Zipporah and her two sons to Moses in the wilderness. He rejoiced at all the Lord had done, confessed that the Lord is greater than all gods, and offered sacrifices (Exodus 18:1–12). Seeing Moses judging the people alone from morning till evening, he advised him to appoint able, God-fearing, honest men to settle smaller cases, and Moses did so (Exodus 18:13–27). Remember. Jethro was an outsider who came to praise Israel’s God, an early sign that the nations would share in Abraham’s blessing. His advice also shows that God’s work is meant to be shared, not carried by one person alone. Exodus 18:11 Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people. Hearing of the exodus, this foreign priest confessed the Lord as the true God. Exodus 18:17-18 Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone. Sound practical advice that led to shared leadership in Israel.

Joshua Moses’ assistant and successor, who led Israel into the promised land. Who. Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, was first called Hoshea; Moses named him Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves” (Numbers 13:16). In Greek his name is Jesus. Do not confuse him with Joshua (also called Jeshua) the high priest after the exile (Ezra 3; Zechariah 3). Their story. He led Israel’s army against Amalek (Exodus 17:8–13) and served as Moses’ assistant, going with him up Mount Sinai (Exodus 24:13). He was one of the twelve spies, and with Caleb urged the people to trust God (Numbers 13–14). God appointed him Moses’ successor (Numbers 27:18–23). He led Israel across the Jordan, saw the walls of Jericho fall, and conquered and divided the land, from about 1406 BC (Joshua 1–21). Before he died at 110 he called Israel to choose whom they would serve (Joshua 24). Remember. Joshua’s courage rested on God’s promise to be with him. He was fallible too: the Gibeonites deceived him because he did not ask counsel of the Lord (Joshua 9:14). His name and work point to Jesus, who brings his people into the true rest that Joshua could not give (Hebrews 4:8–9). Joshua 1:9 Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go. Joshua’s strength was not in himself but in God’s presence with him. Joshua 24:15 But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. Joshua’s last challenge to Israel, and his own settled choice.

Caleb One of the twelve spies, who with Joshua trusted God to give Israel the land. Who. Caleb son of Jephunneh was a leader of the tribe of Judah. He is called a Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12), which probably means his family had joined Israel from outside. He is different from Caleb son of Hezron in 1 Chronicles 2. Their story. Sent with the other spies to explore Canaan, he quieted the people and said they could surely take the land, while ten of the spies spread a bad report (Numbers 13:30–33). Because he followed the Lord fully, God promised that he and Joshua alone of that generation would enter the land (Numbers 14:24, 30). Forty-five years later, aged eighty-five, he asked for the hill country of Hebron, where the giant Anakim lived, and took it (Joshua 14:6–15). He gave his daughter Achsah in marriage to Othniel, who became Israel’s first judge (Judges 1:12–15; 3:9). Remember. Caleb’s faith did not fade with age; he still trusted God’s promise decades later. His wholehearted trust stands against a generation that died in the wilderness through unbelief (Hebrews 3:19). It is not strength but faith in God’s word that inherits the promise. Numbers 14:24 But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land into which he went, and his descendants shall possess it. God honours wholehearted faith. Joshua 14:12 So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said. At eighty-five Caleb still asked for the hardest ground, trusting God’s word.

Korah A Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed up by the earth. Who. Korah son of Izhar was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, and so a cousin of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:18–21). His family already served at the tabernacle, but they were not priests. He is not the same as Korah the son of Esau (Genesis 36:5). Their story. With Dathan, Abiram and On of the tribe of Reuben, and 250 leaders of Israel, Korah rose against Moses and Aaron, claiming that all the congregation was holy and seeking the priesthood for himself (Numbers 16:1–11). Moses left the matter to the Lord. The ground opened and swallowed the rebels and their households, and fire from the Lord consumed the 250 men offering incense (Numbers 16:31–35; 26:10). Yet the sons of Korah did not die (Numbers 26:11). Their descendants later served as singers and gatekeepers at the temple, and several psalms are headed “of the Sons of Korah” (Psalms 42–49). Remember. Korah’s sin was to grasp at an office God had not given him, dressed up as equality. Jude warns of those who perish in Korah’s rebellion (Jude 11). Yet grace shines in his family: Korah’s sons became singers of God’s praise, showing that God’s mercy can reach the children of rebels. Numbers 16:3 They assembled themselves together against Moses and against Aaron and said to them, “You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” Korah’s challenge sounded spiritual, but it rejected the leaders God had chosen. Jude 1:11 Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. The New Testament uses Korah as a warning against rebellion within God’s people.

Balaam A foreign prophet hired to curse Israel, who could speak only the blessing God gave him. Who. Balaam son of Beor was a famous seer from Pethor, near the river Euphrates (Numbers 22:5; Deuteronomy 23:4). He lived near the end of Israel’s forty years in the wilderness. An inscription found at Deir Alla in Jordan, from some centuries later, mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor. Their story. Balak king of Moab sent for him to curse Israel (Numbers 22). On the road the angel of the Lord stood in his way, and his donkey spoke to him (Numbers 22:21–35). Again and again Balaam could only bless Israel, and he foretold a star coming out of Jacob and a sceptre rising out of Israel (Numbers 23–24). Afterwards he advised Moab how to lead Israel into idolatry and sexual sin at Peor (Numbers 25; 31:16; Revelation 2:14). He was killed when Israel fought Midian (Numbers 31:8). Remember. Balaam had true words from God in his mouth but greed in his heart (2 Peter 2:15). No curse can stand against those God has blessed. His prophecy of a star and a sceptre points to Christ, the King from Jacob’s line. Numbers 24:17 I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; Even a hired prophet foretold a coming King, fulfilled in Christ. 2 Peter 2:15 Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, Peter names Balaam’s real sin: the love of money.

Rahab A Canaanite woman of Jericho who hid Israel’s spies by faith and became an ancestor of Jesus. Who. Rahab was a prostitute whose house was built into the city wall of Jericho, at the time of the conquest, about 1406 BC. She is different from “Rahab” used as a poetic name for a sea monster or for Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 51:9). Their story. When Joshua sent two spies to Jericho, Rahab hid them on her roof under stalks of flax and sent the king’s men off in the wrong direction (Joshua 2:1–7). She confessed that the Lord is God in heaven and on earth, and asked the spies to spare her family; they told her to tie a scarlet cord in her window (Joshua 2:8–21). When the walls fell, she and her household were saved and lived among Israel (Joshua 6:22–25). Matthew lists her as the mother of Boaz, and so an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Remember. Rahab lied to protect the spies, and Scripture does not praise the lie; it praises her faith (Hebrews 11:31) and the deeds that showed it (James 2:25). A pagan prostitute was brought into the family line of the Messiah: no one is beyond the reach of God’s grace. Joshua 2:11 for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath. Rahab’s confession of faith in Israel’s God, made in a pagan city. Hebrews 11:31 By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies. She was saved not by her past but by faith. Matthew 1:5 and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Rahab and Ruth, both outsiders, stand in Jesus’ family tree.

Achan An Israelite who stole forbidden plunder from Jericho, bringing defeat on Israel. Who. Achan son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah, lived at the time of the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 7:1). In 1 Chronicles 2:7 he is called Achar, “troubler”. Their story. God had told Israel that everything in Jericho was devoted to him: it was to be destroyed, or, if silver or gold, given to his treasury (Joshua 6:17–19). Achan secretly took a fine cloak, 200 shekels of silver (about 5 pounds or 2.3 kg) and a bar of gold, and hid them under his tent. As a result Israel was defeated at the small town of Ai (Joshua 7:1–5). When the lot fell on him, Achan confessed, and he and his household were stoned in the Valley of Achor, meaning “trouble” (Joshua 7:16–26). Remember. Achan’s sin followed a familiar path: he saw, he coveted, he took, he hid (Joshua 7:21). Hidden sin harms the whole people of God. Yet God later promised to make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (Hosea 2:15). The God who judges sin turns trouble into hope through Christ, who bore the curse for his people. Joshua 7:1 But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel. One man’s sin brought guilt on the whole community. Joshua 7:21 when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. Achan’s confession traces the steps from seeing to coveting to taking.

Deborah A prophetess and judge who called Israel to victory over the Canaanite king Jabin. Who. Deborah, the wife of Lappidoth, judged Israel during the period of the judges (roughly 1375 to 1050 BC; exact dates are uncertain). She sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where Israelites came to her to settle disputes (Judges 4:4–5). She is not the same as Deborah the nurse of Rebekah (Genesis 35:8). Their story. Israel had been oppressed for twenty years by Jabin king of Canaan and his commander Sisera, who had 900 iron chariots. Deborah summoned Barak and gave him God’s command to fight. He would go only if she went too, so she told him the honour would go to a woman (Judges 4:6–9). The Lord routed Sisera’s army by the river Kishon, and Sisera was killed by Jael, the wife of Heber (Judges 4:15–22). Deborah and Barak sang a song of victory (Judges 5), and the land had rest for forty years (Judges 5:31). Remember. Deborah gave all the glory to the Lord, who went out before his people (Judges 4:14). In a dark time God raised up an unlikely leader and won the battle himself. Judges 4:4 Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. Deborah was both a prophetess and a judge, bringing God’s word to his people.

Barak The commander who, at Deborah’s call, led Israel against Sisera’s army. Who. Barak son of Abinoam came from Kedesh in Naphtali, in the north of Israel (Judges 4:6). His name means “lightning”. He served alongside Deborah during the period of the judges. Their story. Deborah told him that the Lord commanded him to gather 10,000 men at Mount Tabor. Barak said he would go only if she came with him; she agreed, but told him the Lord would give Sisera into the hand of a woman (Judges 4:6–9). At Deborah’s word he charged down the mountain, and the Lord threw Sisera’s chariots and army into panic. Barak pursued them, but Sisera fled on foot and was killed by Jael (Judges 4:14–22). Barak sang with Deborah in the song of Judges 5. Remember. Barak’s faith was hesitant, yet Hebrews lists him among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32). God does not wait for perfect faith; he honours weak faith that obeys his word. The victory belonged to the Lord, not to Barak. Judges 4:8 Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” Barak’s hesitation is honestly recorded. Hebrews 11:32 And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets Even so, he is remembered among those who acted by faith.

Gideon The judge, also called Jerubbaal, whom God used with only 300 men to rescue Israel from Midian. Who. Gideon son of Joash, of the clan of Abiezer in the tribe of Manasseh, lived at Ophrah during the period of the judges. After he tore down his father’s altar to Baal he was nicknamed Jerubbaal, “let Baal contend” (Judges 6:32). Abimelech, who later made himself king and murdered his brothers, was Gideon’s son by a concubine (Judges 8:31; 9). Their story. When Midianite raiders had stripped Israel for seven years, the angel of the Lord found Gideon threshing wheat in hiding and called him a mighty man of valour (Judges 6:11–12). Gideon asked for signs with a fleece (Judges 6:36–40). God cut his army from 32,000 to 300 so that Israel could not boast, and routed Midian with trumpets, jars and torches (Judges 7). Gideon refused to be king, but he made a gold ephod (a priestly garment) that Israel came to worship (Judges 8:22–27). Remember. Gideon was fearful and weak, and his last years were marred by idolatry. But God chose weakness on purpose so that the glory would be his (Judges 7:2), as he still does in the gospel (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). Judges 6:15 Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house. Gideon saw only his weakness; God saw what he would do through him. Judges 7:2 The LORD said to Gideon, “The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’ God made the army small so that the victory would plainly be his.

Jephthah A judge from Gilead, rejected by his family, who delivered Israel from the Ammonites but made a rash vow. Who. Jephthah was a mighty warrior from Gilead, east of the Jordan, the son of a man named Gilead by a prostitute. His half-brothers drove him out, and he lived in the land of Tob with a band of worthless men (Judges 11:1–3). Their story. When the Ammonites attacked, the elders of Gilead asked him to lead them, and he became their head (Judges 11:4–11). He argued from history that Israel had a right to the land (Judges 11:12–28). Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, but he also vowed to offer as a burnt offering whatever came out of his house to meet him if he returned victorious (Judges 11:29–31). He defeated Ammon, and his only daughter came out to meet him (Judges 11:34–40). Interpreters differ on whether he sacrificed her or devoted her to lifelong unmarried service of the Lord; many take it that he offered her, which God’s law forbade. He judged Israel six years (Judges 12:7). Remember. Jephthah is named among the faithful (Hebrews 11:32), yet his vow was rash and sinful. God used a flawed outcast, but his story warns against bargaining with God. Only one beloved child was ever rightly offered: the Son God gave for us (Romans 8:32). Judges 11:1 Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. God raised up a deliverer whom his own family had rejected. Judges 11:30-31 And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, “If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD’s, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.” A vow made in haste, which brought grief on his own house.

Samson A Nazirite judge of enormous strength who fought the Philistines but was ruled by his desires. Who. Samson son of Manoah, of the tribe of Dan, was born to a woman who had been unable to have children, after the angel of the Lord announced his birth (Judges 13). He was to be a Nazirite (someone set apart to God) from birth, never cutting his hair. He judged Israel twenty years under Philistine rule, probably about 1100 BC (Judges 15:20). Their story. He married a Philistine woman of Timnah against his parents’ wishes (Judges 14). With the Spirit of the Lord upon him he tore a lion apart, struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone (Judges 15:14–15) and carried off the gates of Gaza (Judges 16:1–3). Delilah coaxed from him the secret of his strength; his head was shaved, and the Philistines blinded him (Judges 16:4–21). In the temple of their god Dagon he prayed one last time and pulled down the pillars, killing more at his death than in his life (Judges 16:23–30). Remember. Samson was a deeply flawed man who broke his vows and followed his eyes, yet God used him and he is counted among the faithful (Hebrews 11:32). In his death he struck down the enemies of God’s people, a faint picture of Christ, who conquered by his death. Judges 13:5 for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines. Samson was set apart by God before birth to begin Israel’s rescue. Judges 16:28 Then Samson called to the LORD and said, “O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.” Blind and humbled, Samson finally turned to the Lord in prayer.

Delilah The woman Samson loved, who betrayed him to the Philistines for money. Who. Delilah lived in the Valley of Sorek, on the border between Israel and the land of the Philistines, about 1100 BC (Judges 16:4). The Bible does not say whether she was a Philistine or an Israelite. She is the only woman in Samson’s story whose name is given. Their story. The lords of the Philistines each offered her 1,100 pieces of silver to find out the secret of Samson’s strength (Judges 16:5). Three times she asked, and three times he lied, while Philistines waited in hiding to seize him. She pressed him day after day until he told her about his uncut hair. While he slept she had his head shaved; his strength left him, because the Lord had left him, and the Philistines seized and blinded him (Judges 16:6–21). Remember. Delilah’s name has come to stand for a treacherous lover. Her story shows how betrayal for money destroys, as Judas would betray Jesus for silver (Matthew 26:14–16). It also shows Samson’s folly: he played with sin until it bound him. Judges 16:5 Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver. Delilah’s betrayal was bought with money. Judges 16:20 And she said, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” And he awoke from his sleep and said, “I will go out as at other times and shake myself free.” But he did not know that the LORD had left him. Samson’s real loss was not his hair but the Lord’s presence.

Ruth A Moabite widow who came to trust Israel’s God and became the great-grandmother of King David. Who. Ruth lived in the days of the judges (Ruth 1:1), probably about 1100 BC. She was a woman of Moab who married Mahlon, a son of Elimelech and Naomi, Israelites from Bethlehem who had moved to Moab during a famine. Their story. When Naomi’s husband and both sons died, Ruth refused to leave her, binding herself to Naomi, her people and her God (Ruth 1:16–17). In Bethlehem she gleaned (gathered the grain left by the reapers) in the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, who treated her with kindness (Ruth 2). At Naomi’s suggestion she asked Boaz at the threshing floor to act as their redeemer (Ruth 3). Boaz married her, and their son Obed became the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:13–17). Remember. Ruth’s loyal, steadfast love mirrors God’s own. A woman from Moab, a people barred from Israel’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), took refuge under God’s wings and was brought into the line of Christ (Matthew 1:5). The good news was always meant for the nations. Ruth 1:16 Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Ruth’s famous pledge is a confession of faith in Israel’s God. Ruth 2:12 The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge! Boaz sees that Ruth has come to shelter under the Lord himself.

Naomi An Israelite widow from Bethlehem whose bitterness was turned to joy through Ruth and Boaz. Who. Naomi, whose name means “pleasant”, was the wife of Elimelech of Bethlehem in Judah, in the days of the judges. Her sons were Mahlon and Chilion. Their story. Because of famine the family moved to Moab, where her sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Over about ten years Elimelech and both sons died (Ruth 1:1–5). Naomi returned to Bethlehem with Ruth and told the women to call her Mara, “bitter” (Ruth 1:19–21). She saw God’s kindness when Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz, one of their family redeemers (Ruth 2:20), and she guided Ruth to approach him (Ruth 3). When Ruth bore Obed, the women blessed the Lord, who had not left Naomi without a redeemer, and she cared for the child (Ruth 4:14–17). Remember. Naomi spoke honestly of her grief, even laying it at God’s door, and God did not abandon her. The one she thought had emptied her was quietly filling her again. Her redeemer’s line led to David and to Christ, the Redeemer of all who trust him. Ruth 1:20-21 Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Naomi’s honest lament is recorded in Scripture without rebuke. Ruth 4:14 Then the women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel! The story ends with Naomi’s emptiness filled by God’s provision.

Boaz A godly landowner of Bethlehem who acted as kinsman-redeemer and married Ruth. Who. Boaz was a wealthy man of Bethlehem, a relative of Naomi’s husband Elimelech, in the days of the judges. Matthew names his mother as Rahab (Matthew 1:5). He was the great-grandfather of King David. Their story. Boaz noticed Ruth gleaning in his field, blessed her, and quietly made sure she gathered plenty (Ruth 2). When Ruth asked him at the threshing floor to spread his wings over her as a redeemer, he promised to act (Ruth 3). In Israel a close relative, the kinsman-redeemer, could buy back family land and provide for a dead relative’s widow so that his name would not die out. A nearer relative refused, so Boaz bought the land and took Ruth as his wife before witnesses at the town gate (Ruth 4:1–12). Their son was Obed (Ruth 4:13–17). Remember. Boaz shows what a redeemer is: a relative who freely pays the price to rescue family in need. He is a clear picture of Christ, who became our kinsman by taking our flesh and redeemed us at his own cost. Ruth 4:10 Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, Boaz willingly paid the cost of redeeming the family.

Eli The priest at Shiloh in Samuel’s childhood, who failed to restrain his wicked sons. Who. Eli was the priest at the tabernacle at Shiloh and judged Israel for forty years near the end of the period of the judges, about 1100 BC (1 Samuel 4:18). He was descended from Aaron. His sons Hophni and Phinehas also served as priests. Their story. Eli at first mistook Hannah’s silent prayer for drunkenness, then blessed her (1 Samuel 1:12–17). He brought up the boy Samuel and taught him how to answer when the Lord called (1 Samuel 3:8–9). His sons took the best of the sacrifices for themselves and lay with the women who served at the tabernacle, but Eli rebuked them only mildly (1 Samuel 2:12–25). A man of God, and then Samuel, announced judgment on his house (1 Samuel 2:27–36; 3:11–18). When news came that the ark was captured and both sons killed, Eli fell backwards and died, aged ninety-eight (1 Samuel 4:12–18). Remember. Eli bowed humbly to God’s word (1 Samuel 3:18), yet he honoured his sons above the Lord (1 Samuel 2:29). Love at home must include correction. God promised to raise up a faithful priest in place of Eli’s line (1 Samuel 2:35), a promise that finds its fullest answer in Christ. 1 Samuel 2:12 Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD. Priests by birth, they did not know God at all. 1 Samuel 3:13 And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them. Eli’s sin was knowing the evil and failing to stop it.

Hannah A woman unable to have children who prayed for a son, received Samuel, and gave him back to the Lord. Who. Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah, an Ephraimite from Ramathaim (Ramah), near the end of the period of the judges, about 1100 BC. She is not the same as Anna the prophetess in Luke 2, though their names are related. Their story. Childless, and provoked year after year by Elkanah’s other wife Peninnah, Hannah poured out her soul to the Lord at Shiloh. She vowed that if he gave her a son, she would give him to the Lord all his life (1 Samuel 1:1–11). Eli thought she was drunk, then blessed her (1 Samuel 1:12–18). She bore Samuel, and when he was weaned she brought him to serve at the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:19–28). Her song praises the God who humbles the proud and lifts the lowly (1 Samuel 2:1–10). God later gave her three more sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21). Remember. Hannah took her sorrow to God rather than letting it turn to bitterness. Her song ends with the Lord’s king and anointed (1 Samuel 2:10), and Mary’s song echoes it (Luke 1:46–55): the God who heard Hannah was preparing the way for Christ. 1 Samuel 1:27 For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Hannah’s son was an answer to prayer, and she gave him back to God. 1 Samuel 2:2 There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God. Her song turns from her own joy to the greatness of God.

Samuel The last of the judges, a prophet and priestly leader who anointed Israel’s first two kings. Who. Samuel was the son of Elkanah and Hannah, born in answer to prayer about 1100 BC. He was a Levite by descent (1 Chronicles 6:26–28) and served as prophet, judge and leader of worship. His home was at Ramah. Their story. Given to the Lord as a child, he grew up under Eli at Shiloh, where the Lord called him by name (1 Samuel 3). He led Israel in repentance and to victory over the Philistines at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7). When the people demanded a king, he warned them, but at God’s command anointed Saul (1 Samuel 8–10). When Saul disobeyed, Samuel declared that God had rejected him (1 Samuel 13; 15), and he anointed the young David (1 Samuel 16). Sadly, his own sons did not walk in his ways (1 Samuel 8:3). When he died, all Israel mourned him (1 Samuel 25:1). Remember. Samuel was a man of prayer and integrity who would not stop praying for a rebellious people (1 Samuel 12:23). He prepared the way for David, as John the Baptist would prepare the way for David’s greater Son. 1 Samuel 3:10 And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel said, “Speak, for your servant hears.” Samuel’s ministry began with listening to God. 1 Samuel 15:22 Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. Samuel’s word to Saul: God wants obedience, not religious show.

Saul Saul was the first king of Israel, chosen by God and later rejected for his disobedience. Who. Saul was the son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, a tall and handsome young man. He became Israel’s first king in about 1050 BC and reigned for many years (Acts 13:21 gives forty). His sons included Jonathan, and his daughters included Michal, David’s first wife. Do not confuse him with Saul of Tarsus, the apostle Paul, who also came from Benjamin. Their story. Samuel anointed him privately and he was then chosen by lot (1 Samuel 9–10). He began well, rescuing the town of Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11). But he offered a sacrifice he had no right to offer (1 Samuel 13) and spared what God had told him to destroy (1 Samuel 15), so God rejected him as king. Jealous of David, he tried again and again to kill him (1 Samuel 18–26). He consulted a medium at Endor, and died by his own sword on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 28; 31). Remember. Saul looked like a king but would not obey God from the heart. Outward religion cannot replace listening to God’s word. Israel needed a king after God’s own heart, and in the end only Christ is that King perfectly. 1 Samuel 15:22 Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
