Samuel’s words to Saul after he spared the Amalekite king and the best of the flocks. 1 Samuel 13:14 The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people God announces that Saul’s line will not continue and that another will take his place.

Jonathan Jonathan was King Saul’s eldest son, a brave warrior and David’s loyal friend. Who. Jonathan was the son of Saul, Israel’s first king, and the natural heir to the throne, around 1050–1010 BC. Several other men in the Bible share his name, such as a son of the priest Abiathar (2 Samuel 15:27) and Moses’ grandson who became a priest of idols (Judges 18:30); this card is about Saul’s son. Their story. With only his armour-bearer he attacked a Philistine outpost, trusting the LORD to save (1 Samuel 14). When David killed Goliath, Jonathan loved him “as his own soul” and made a covenant with him, giving him his robe and weapons (1 Samuel 18:1–4). He warned David of Saul’s plans and gladly accepted that David, not he, would be king (1 Samuel 20; 23:16–18). He died with his father on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31), and David mourned him deeply (2 Samuel 1) and later showed kindness to his lame son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9). Remember. Jonathan gave up his own claim to the throne for the one God had chosen. That is a picture of true faith and friendship: glad to bow to God’s anointed King, as believers gladly bow to Christ. 1 Samuel 18:1 the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. The start of one of the Bible’s great friendships, just after David’s victory over Goliath. 1 Samuel 14:6 for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few. Jonathan’s confidence before attacking the Philistine garrison with only one companion.

David David was the shepherd boy who became Israel’s greatest king and the ancestor of Jesus Christ. Who. David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, from the tribe of Judah. He reigned about 1010–970 BC: seven and a half years at Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:4–5). His wives included Michal, Abigail and Bathsheba, and his sons included Absalom and Solomon. He wrote many of the Psalms. Their story. Samuel anointed him while he was still a shepherd (1 Samuel 16), and he killed Goliath in the LORD’s name (1 Samuel 17). For years he fled from Saul, yet twice refused to kill him (1 Samuel 18–26). He became king, captured Jerusalem and brought the ark there (2 Samuel 2–6). God promised him a house and a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7). He then committed adultery with Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11). Rebuked by Nathan, he repented (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51), but sorrow followed in his family, including Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 13–18). Remember. David was a man after God’s heart, yet a great sinner who found great mercy. God kept his promise: Jesus is the Son of David whose kingdom has no end. 1 Samuel 16:7 For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart. Spoken when Samuel came to Jesse’s sons and God passed over the older brothers for David. 2 Samuel 7:16 And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever. God’s covenant promise to David, fulfilled in Jesus, the everlasting King. Psalm 51:10 Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. David’s prayer of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba.

Michal Michal was King Saul’s younger daughter and David’s first wife. Who. Michal was the daughter of Saul and the sister of Jonathan. She married David while he was still serving in Saul’s court, around 1020 BC. Saul hoped the marriage would be a trap that got David killed by the Philistines. Their story. Michal loved David (1 Samuel 18:20–27), and when Saul sent men to kill him she let him down through a window and put an idol in his bed to fool them (1 Samuel 19:11–17). While David was a fugitive, Saul gave her to another man, Palti (1 Samuel 25:44). After Saul’s death David demanded her back, and her second husband followed her weeping (2 Samuel 3:13–16). When David danced with all his might as the ark came into Jerusalem, Michal despised him and mocked him, and she had no child to the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:16–23). Remember. Michal’s life was bent by the politics of two kings, and there is real sadness in it. Yet her final scene warns us against scorning wholehearted joy in God. Worship that seems undignified to others may be precious to him. 1 Samuel 18:20 Now Saul’s daughter Michal loved David. Her love was real, though her father tried to use it against David. 2 Samuel 6:16 Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. Her contempt for David’s joyful worship as the ark arrived.

Abigail Abigail was a wise woman who stopped David from taking revenge and later became his wife. Who. Abigail was the wife of Nabal, a rich but harsh sheep owner in Carmel, in the south of Judah, around 1015 BC. Scripture calls her “discerning and beautiful” (1 Samuel 25:3). After Nabal’s death she married David and bore him a son, Chileab, also called Daniel (2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1). David’s sister was also called Abigail (1 Chronicles 2:16), a different woman. Their story. While hiding from Saul, David’s men had protected Nabal’s flocks, but Nabal insulted them when they asked for food. David set out to kill every male in Nabal’s household. Abigail quickly loaded donkeys with food, met David on the way, took the blame on herself and reminded him of God’s promises to him. David blessed God for sending her. Ten days later the LORD struck Nabal and he died (1 Samuel 25). Later she was captured by Amalekites at Ziklag and rescued by David (1 Samuel 30:5, 18). Remember. Abigail’s humble, wise words turned a king away from sin. She stood between an angry king and a guilty household, a small picture of the greater peacemaking of Christ. 1 Samuel 25:32 Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! David sees God’s hand in Abigail’s coming. 1 Samuel 25:33 Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand! Her wisdom kept David from murder and from taking revenge into his own hands.

Bathsheba Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah whom David took in adultery, and later the mother of King Solomon. Who. Bathsheba was the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of David’s soldiers (2 Samuel 11:3). She lived in Jerusalem in about 1000 BC. After Uriah’s death she became David’s wife and the mother of Solomon. Their story. While Uriah was at war, David saw her bathing, sent for her and slept with her, and she became pregnant (2 Samuel 11:1–5). David arranged Uriah’s death and married her, but the child died (2 Samuel 11–12). God then gave them Solomon, whom the LORD loved (2 Samuel 12:24–25). Years later, with the prophet Nathan, she reminded the aged David of his promise that Solomon would be king (1 Kings 1). As queen mother she was honoured by Solomon (1 Kings 2:19). Remember. The Bible lays the blame for this sin at David’s door, not hers, and does not hide the grief it brought her. Matthew names her in Jesus’ family line as “the wife of Uriah”, a reminder that God works his grace through broken and sinful histories. 2 Samuel 11:27 But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD. Scripture places the guilt squarely on David. Matthew 1:6 And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, Bathsheba is remembered in the genealogy of Jesus.

Uriah the Hittite Uriah was a loyal soldier in David’s army whom David had killed to cover his adultery with Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba. Who. Uriah was a Hittite by descent, from a people who had lived in Canaan before Israel, yet he served Israel’s God and King. He was one of David’s thirty mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39) and the husband of Bathsheba, around 1000 BC. His name probably means “the LORD is my light”. Do not confuse him with Uriah the priest in King Ahaz’s day (2 Kings 16:10–16) or Uriah the prophet killed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20–23). Their story. While Uriah fought the Ammonites, David slept with his wife. To hide her pregnancy, David called him home and urged him to go to his house, but Uriah would not enjoy comforts while the ark and the army were in tents. David then sent him back carrying a letter that ordered Joab to put him in the hardest fighting and leave him to die, and so he was killed (2 Samuel 11). Remember. The foreigner was more faithful than the king of Israel. Uriah’s death shows how one sin leads to another. Yet the God who saw it all also forgave David when he repented (2 Samuel 12:13). 2 Samuel 11:11 The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Uriah’s reason for refusing to go home: he would not rest while his comrades were at war.

Nathan Nathan was a prophet in King David’s court who brought him both God’s great promise and God’s rebuke. Who. Nathan was a prophet in Jerusalem during the reigns of David and the early years of Solomon, around 1000–970 BC. He also kept written records of these kings (1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29). He is a different person from Nathan the son of David (2 Samuel 5:14), through whom Luke traces Jesus’ line (Luke 3:31). Their story. When David wanted to build a house for God, Nathan brought God’s word that God would instead build David a house, a royal line whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7). After David’s sin with Bathsheba, Nathan told him a story of a rich man who stole a poor man’s only lamb, and when David burned with anger, Nathan said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:1–14). He gave the baby Solomon the name Jedidiah, “loved by the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:25), and later made sure Solomon became king (1 Kings 1). Remember. Nathan spoke the truth to a powerful king, with wisdom and courage. Loving rebuke can lead to repentance, and with it comes God’s forgiveness. 2 Samuel 12:7 Nathan said to David, “You are the man! The moment Nathan turned his story on the king. 2 Samuel 12:13 The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nathan’s word of forgiveness after David confessed.

Absalom Absalom was King David’s handsome son who killed his brother and led a rebellion against his father. Who. Absalom was David’s third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, the daughter of the king of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3), around 1000 BC. He was famous for his good looks and his thick hair (2 Samuel 14:25–26). Their story. When his half-brother Amnon raped his sister Tamar and David did nothing, Absalom waited two years and had Amnon killed. He fled to Geshur for three years (2 Samuel 13). Joab arranged his return, but David kept him at a distance (2 Samuel 14). Absalom then won people over with flattery and declared himself king at Hebron, and David fled Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15–16). In the battle in the forest of Ephraim his head was caught in an oak, and Joab killed him against David’s orders (2 Samuel 18). David wept bitterly for him. Remember. Absalom’s story shows the bitter fruit of David’s own sin in his family, and the danger of pride and stolen loyalty. David wished he could have died instead of his rebel son. Christ did what David could only wish: he died in the place of rebels. 2 Samuel 15:6 So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. How Absalom prepared his rebellion: by charm and false promises at the city gate. 2 Samuel 18:33 O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son! David’s grief when he heard of Absalom’s death.

Joab Joab was David’s nephew and the ruthless commander of his army. Who. Joab was the son of Zeruiah, David’s sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), and brother of Abishai and Asahel. He commanded David’s army for most of David’s reign, around 1000–970 BC, after leading the capture of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 11:6). Their story. He was a skilful and loyal soldier, but violent and self-willed. He murdered Abner in revenge for his brother Asahel (2 Samuel 3:27). He carried out David’s order to have Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11). He brought Absalom back to Jerusalem, then killed him against David’s command (2 Samuel 14; 18:14), and sternly told the grieving king to thank his troops (2 Samuel 19:5–7). He murdered Amasa, another commander (2 Samuel 20:10), and objected to David’s census (2 Samuel 24:3). In the end he backed Adonijah rather than Solomon, and Solomon had him put to death (1 Kings 1–2). Remember. Joab served the king when it suited him and did evil to get his way. Usefulness to God’s cause is no substitute for a heart that obeys God. 1 Kings 2:5 Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed David’s charge to Solomon remembers Joab’s murders. 2 Samuel 18:14 And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak. Joab disobeys David’s order to deal gently with Absalom.

Solomon Solomon was David’s son, the wise king who built the temple in Jerusalem and later turned to other gods. Who. Solomon was the son of David and Bathsheba, also named Jedidiah, “loved by the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:24–25). He reigned over all Israel for forty years, about 970–931 BC. Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs are linked with him, and two of the Psalms bear his name (72 and 127). Their story. At the start of his reign he asked God for wisdom to rule, and God gave him wisdom, riches and honour (1 Kings 3). He built the temple and dedicated it with a great prayer (1 Kings 6–8). His wisdom and wealth became famous, and the queen of Sheba came to test him (1 Kings 4; 10). But he married many foreign wives, who turned his heart to their gods, and God said the kingdom would be torn from his son (1 Kings 11). Remember. Gifts, even wisdom, do not keep a heart faithful; only God’s grace does. Jesus said that “something greater than Solomon is here”: the truly wise King who builds the true temple, his people. 1 Kings 3:9 Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil Solomon’s humble request at the start of his reign. 1 Kings 11:4 For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods The sad end of a wise man who did not guard his heart. Matthew 12:42 and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. Jesus points to himself as the greater King of wisdom.

Rehoboam Rehoboam was Solomon’s son, whose harsh answer to the people split the kingdom of Israel in two. Who. Rehoboam was the son of Solomon and Naamah the Ammonite (1 Kings 14:21). He became king at forty-one and reigned seventeen years over Judah, about 931–913 BC. He was the first king of the southern kingdom of Judah after the division. Their story. At Shechem the northern tribes asked him to lighten the heavy load Solomon had laid on them. He rejected the advice of the older men and followed his young friends, promising even heavier burdens. Ten tribes broke away and made Jeroboam their king (1 Kings 12:1–20). God stopped him from going to war against them (1 Kings 12:21–24). Judah fell into idolatry under him, and Shishak king of Egypt plundered the temple and palace treasures (1 Kings 14:21–28). When he humbled himself, God did not destroy him completely (2 Chronicles 12). Remember. Pride and foolish advice cost Rehoboam most of his kingdom. Yet even this was God fulfilling his word, and God kept a lamp burning for David in Jerusalem, so that the promised King would come from David’s line. 1 Kings 12:14 My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. Rehoboam’s proud answer that split the kingdom. 1 Kings 12:15 for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word Even a foolish decision served God’s purpose and promise.

Jeroboam son of Nebat Jeroboam son of Nebat was the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, who set up golden calves for worship. Who. Jeroboam was an Ephraimite whom Solomon had put in charge of forced labour (1 Kings 11:26–28). He reigned over the ten northern tribes for twenty-two years, about 931–910 BC. He is different from Jeroboam II, son of Joash, who reigned in Israel about 793–753 BC (2 Kings 14:23–29), in the days of Jonah, Hosea and Amos. Their story. The prophet Ahijah tore his new cloak into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten, as a sign that God would give him ten tribes (1 Kings 11:29–39). He fled to Egypt from Solomon and came back to be made king when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:1–20). Afraid that his people would return to Jerusalem to worship, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, appointed his own priests and invented his own feast (1 Kings 12:25–33). A prophet from Judah condemned his altar (1 Kings 13), and his son died as Ahijah warned (1 Kings 14). Remember. Jeroboam chose political safety over true worship. For generations afterwards kings were measured against “Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin”. Worship invented for convenience leads people away from God. 1 Kings 11:31 Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes God’s promise to Jeroboam through Ahijah’s torn cloak. 1 Kings 12:28 So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. Jeroboam’s great sin, which shaped the northern kingdom’s whole history.

Ahab Ahab was a wicked king of Israel who, with his wife Jezebel, promoted the worship of Baal. Who. Ahab was the son of Omri and reigned over the northern kingdom of Israel from Samaria for twenty-two years, about 874–853 BC. His wife was Jezebel. He is not the false prophet Ahab of Jeremiah 29:21. Their story. Ahab built a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria (1 Kings 16:29–33). God sent a drought through Elijah, and on Mount Carmel fire from heaven showed that the LORD is God (1 Kings 17–18). He won battles against Ben-hadad of Syria but let him go (1 Kings 20). When Jezebel had Naboth killed so Ahab could take his vineyard, Elijah pronounced judgment; Ahab humbled himself, and God delayed the disaster (1 Kings 21). Ignoring the prophet Micaiah, he went to battle at Ramoth-gilead, was struck by an arrow shot at random, and died, and dogs licked his blood as foretold (1 Kings 22). Remember. Ahab was weak and wicked, yet God was patient with him, even noticing his brief humbling. No disguise could hide him from God’s word. God’s judgment is sure, and so is his readiness to show mercy to the humble. 1 Kings 16:30 And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him. Scripture’s summary of his reign. 1 Kings 21:29 Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Even toward Ahab, God responds to humbling with mercy.

Jezebel Jezebel was the foreign queen of Israel, Ahab’s wife, who led the nation into Baal worship and persecuted God’s prophets. Who. Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians on the coast north of Israel (1 Kings 16:31). She married King Ahab and was queen in Samaria in the ninth century BC, about 874–853 BC, and queen mother afterwards. Her daughter Athaliah later seized the throne of Judah (2 Kings 8:18, 26; 11). Their story. She brought Baal worship into Israel, supported hundreds of his prophets and killed the LORD’s prophets (1 Kings 18:4, 19). After Elijah’s victory on Mount Carmel she swore to kill him, and he fled (1 Kings 19:1–3). She arranged false witnesses so that Naboth was stoned and Ahab could have his vineyard (1 Kings 21). Years later, when Jehu came to Jezreel, she painted her eyes and mocked him; her servants threw her from a window, and dogs ate her body, as Elijah had said (2 Kings 9:30–37). Remember. Jezebel shows how dangerous power is when it is used to drive out God’s word. Her name became a byword: Jesus uses it for a false teacher in the church at Thyatira (Revelation 2:20). The proud may rage, but God’s word stands. 1 Kings 21:25 There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited. Jezebel stirred up her husband’s evil. 1 Kings 19:2 So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow. Her threat to Elijah after the prophets of Baal were killed.

Elijah Elijah was a bold prophet who called Israel back to the LORD in the days of King Ahab and was taken up to heaven without dying. Who. Elijah the Tishbite came from Gilead, east of the Jordan (1 Kings 17:1), and prophesied in the northern kingdom in the ninth century BC, under Ahab and his son Ahaziah. His name means “my God is the LORD”. Their story. He announced a drought, was fed by ravens, and raised a widow’s son at Zarephath (1 Kings 17). On Mount Carmel he challenged the prophets of Baal, and the LORD answered by fire (1 Kings 18). Afraid of Jezebel, he fled to Mount Horeb, where God met him in a low whisper and gave him new work (1 Kings 19). He called Elisha to follow him and condemned Ahab for Naboth’s murder (1 Kings 19; 21). He was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Remember. Elijah was “a man with a nature like ours”, brave and also discouraged, and God heard his prayers. Malachi promised that Elijah would come again; Jesus said this was fulfilled in John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ (Matthew 11:14). Elijah also appeared with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). 1 Kings 18:21 How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him. Elijah’s challenge to the people on Mount Carmel. James 5:17 Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain James uses Elijah to encourage ordinary believers to pray. Malachi 4:5 Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. The promise fulfilled in John the Baptist.

Elisha Elisha was Elijah’s successor, a prophet whose many miracles showed God’s care for Israel and even for foreigners. Who. Elisha was the son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah. Elijah found him ploughing and threw his cloak over him (1 Kings 19:16–21). He prophesied in the northern kingdom in the ninth century BC, through the reigns of several kings of Israel. His name means “God saves”. Their story. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit, took up his cloak and parted the Jordan (2 Kings 2). He multiplied a poor widow’s oil, raised the Shunammite woman’s son, and fed a hundred men with a little bread (2 Kings 4). He cleansed Naaman the Syrian of leprosy (2 Kings 5), made an axe head float, and prayed that his frightened servant would see the hills full of fiery chariots (2 Kings 6). He sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu king (2 Kings 9). Even after his death, a dead man thrown into his grave came to life (2 Kings 13:20–21). Remember. Elisha’s miracles were mostly quiet acts of mercy, often for the poor and the outsider. They look forward to Jesus, who fed crowds, cleansed lepers and raised the dead. 2 Kings 2:9 Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me. Elisha asks to be Elijah’s true heir in ministry. 2 Kings 6:17 the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. God’s unseen protection of his servant, revealed in answer to prayer.

Naaman Naaman was a Syrian army commander who was healed of leprosy when he washed in the Jordan at Elisha’s word. Who. Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Syria (Aram), Israel’s enemy to the north-east, in Elisha’s time, the ninth century BC. He was a great and honoured man, but he had leprosy, a word the Bible uses for various serious skin diseases (2 Kings 5:1). Their story. A young Israelite girl, taken captive and serving his wife, told them of the prophet in Samaria. Naaman went to Elisha with rich gifts, but Elisha simply sent word that he should wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was angry, thinking the rivers of Damascus were better, but his servants persuaded him. He washed and his flesh became like a little child’s. He declared that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, and refused to worship any other god. Elisha’s servant Gehazi greedily took gifts from him and was struck with his leprosy (2 Kings 5). Remember. Naaman had to lay down his pride and receive healing as a free gift. Jesus pointed to him to show that God’s grace reaches outsiders (Luke 4:27). Salvation comes the same way: humbly receiving what God gives. 2 Kings 5:14 and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean. Naaman is healed when he obeys the simple word of God. Luke 4:27 And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. Jesus uses Naaman to show God’s grace to the nations.

Jehu Jehu was an army commander anointed king of Israel to wipe out the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal. Who. Jehu was the son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi (2 Kings 9:2), a commander in Israel’s army. He reigned twenty-eight years, about 841–814 BC, and founded the longest-ruling family of kings in the northern kingdom. Do not confuse him with Jehu son of Hanani, a prophet (1 Kings 16:1; 2 Chronicles 19:2). An Assyrian monument, the Black Obelisk, probably shows Jehu or his envoy bowing to King Shalmaneser III. Their story. A young prophet sent by Elisha anointed him at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 9:1–13). Driving “furiously”, he killed Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah (2 Kings 9:14–29). He had Jezebel thrown from a window (2 Kings 9:30–37), killed Ahab’s seventy sons (2 Kings 10:1–11), and destroyed the worshippers and temple of Baal in Samaria (2 Kings 10:18–28). But he kept Jeroboam’s golden calves (2 Kings 10:29). Remember. Jehu carried out God’s judgment, and God rewarded him, but his zeal stopped short of wholehearted obedience. Zeal against other people’s sins is not the same as a heart that walks in God’s law. 2 Kings 10:30 Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes God recognises what Jehu did in obedience. 2 Kings 10:31 But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. Yet his obedience was only partial.

Hezekiah Hezekiah was a godly king of Judah who reformed worship and trusted the LORD when the Assyrians besieged Jerusalem. Who. Hezekiah was the son of the wicked King Ahaz and the father of Manasseh. He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, probably about 715–686 BC (scholars differ on the exact dates). The prophets Isaiah and Micah ministered in his day. Their story. He removed the high places and broke in pieces the bronze serpent Moses had made, because people were burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). He cleansed the temple and held a great Passover (2 Chronicles 29–30). When Sennacherib king of Assyria invaded in 701 BC and mocked the LORD, Hezekiah spread the letter before God and prayed; the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp, and Jerusalem was saved (2 Kings 18–19; Isaiah 36–37). When he was ill, God added fifteen years to his life (2 Kings 20:1–11). But he proudly showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon, and Isaiah foretold the exile (2 Kings 20:12–19). He also built a tunnel to bring water into the city (2 Kings 20:20). Remember. Hezekiah shows what trust in God looks like under pressure. Even good kings fail, which is why we need a perfect King. 2 Kings 18:5 He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him, nor among those who were before him. Hezekiah’s special mark was trust in the LORD. 2 Kings 19:19 So now, O LORD our God, save us, please, from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, O LORD, are God alone. His prayer when Jerusalem was threatened by Assyria.

Josiah Josiah was the boy king of Judah who renewed the covenant after the Book of the Law was found in the temple. Who. Josiah was the son of Amon and the grandson of Manasseh. He became king at the age of eight and reigned thirty-one years, about 640–609 BC (2 Kings 22:1). Jeremiah, Zephaniah and the prophetess Huldah lived in his day. About three hundred years earlier a prophet had named him as the king who would defile Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel (1 Kings 13:2). Their story. While the temple was being repaired, the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law, probably in 622 BC. When it was read to Josiah he tore his clothes in grief and sent to Huldah, who said judgment would come but not in his days (2 Kings 22). He read the law to the people, renewed the covenant, destroyed idols and shrines throughout the land, including the altar at Bethel, and kept a great Passover (2 Kings 23:1–25). He was killed at Megiddo fighting Pharaoh Neco of Egypt (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:20–25). Remember. Josiah shows the power of God’s word to bring true reform. Yet his reforms could not change the nation’s heart, and judgment still came; God’s people needed the new covenant that writes his law on the heart. 2 Kings 22:19 because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the LORD God’s word through Huldah about Josiah’s response to the law. 2 Kings 23:25 Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might Scripture’s high praise of Josiah.

Manasseh, king of Judah Manasseh was the most wicked king of Judah, who later humbled himself and found mercy. Who. Manasseh was the son of the godly King Hezekiah. He became king at twelve and reigned fifty-five years, longer than any other king of Judah, about 697–642 BC (probably including some years ruling alongside his father). He is not Manasseh the son of Joseph, father of the tribe of Manasseh (Genesis 41:51). Their story. He rebuilt the high places his father had destroyed, put up altars to Baal and to the stars in the temple courts, burned his son as an offering, practised sorcery and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood (2 Kings 21:1–16). Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was killed under him. Because of his sins God declared that Jerusalem would fall (2 Kings 21:10–15; 24:3–4). The Assyrians took him captive to Babylon with hooks. In his distress he humbled himself and prayed, and God brought him back to Jerusalem; he then removed foreign gods from the temple (2 Chronicles 33:10–17). Remember. No sinner is beyond the reach of God’s mercy when he humbles himself and prays. Yet Manasseh’s sins still left lasting damage on his nation. Grace forgives the sinner, even when it does not remove every consequence. 2 Kings 21:9 Manasseh led them astray to do more evil than the nations had done whom the LORD destroyed before the people of Israel. The depth of his wickedness. 2 Chronicles 33:13 He prayed to him, and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God. God’s astonishing mercy to the repentant king.

Isaiah Isaiah was a great prophet in Jerusalem who foretold both judgment and the coming of the suffering Servant, Jesus Christ. Who. Isaiah was the son of Amoz (not the prophet Amos). He prophesied in Jerusalem in the days of Kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1), from about 740 BC to after 700 BC. His wife is called “the prophetess”, and his two sons had names that were signs to the nation (Isaiah 7:3; 8:3). Their story. In the year King Uzziah died he saw the LORD high and lifted up in the temple, was cleansed of his sin and was sent to speak (Isaiah 6). He gave King Ahaz the sign of Immanuel, the child born of a virgin (Isaiah 7:14). He encouraged King Hezekiah when the Assyrians besieged Jerusalem, and foretold the Babylonian exile (Isaiah 36–39). The book that bears his name looks far ahead to comfort for God’s people, to the Servant of the LORD who suffers for sinners (Isaiah 52:13–53:12), and to new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). Remember. Isaiah is quoted in the New Testament more than almost any other prophet. He saw Christ’s glory (John 12:41), and his words about the suffering Servant are among the clearest pictures of the cross in the Old Testament. Isaiah 6:8 Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? God’s call after Isaiah’s vision of his holiness. Isaiah 53:5 But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. Isaiah’s great prophecy of Christ’s death in the place of sinners.

Jeremiah Jeremiah was the prophet who warned Judah for about forty years before Jerusalem fell, and promised a new covenant. Who. Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, from a family of priests at Anathoth in the land of Benjamin (Jeremiah 1:1). God called him as a young man in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BC, and he prophesied until after Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC. He is often called “the weeping prophet”, and Lamentations is traditionally linked with him. His scribe was Baruch. Their story. He preached against trust in the temple while the people lived wickedly (Jeremiah 7). God told him not to marry, as a sign of coming disaster (Jeremiah 16:2). He was beaten and put in the stocks (Jeremiah 20:2), his scroll was burned by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 36), and he was thrown into a muddy cistern and rescued by Ebed-melech (Jeremiah 38). After the fall of Jerusalem he was taken to Egypt against his will (Jeremiah 43). Remember. Jeremiah was faithful through rejection and grief. In the darkest days he promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on his people’s hearts, which Jesus brought in through his blood (Luke 22:20). Jeremiah 1:5 Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations. God’s call to the young Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31:33 I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. The promise of the new covenant, fulfilled in Christ.

Jonah Jonah was the prophet who ran from God’s call to Nineveh, was swallowed by a great fish, and was angry when God showed mercy. Who. Jonah was the son of Amittai from Gath-hepher in Galilee. He prophesied in the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel, in the eighth century BC, and foretold that king’s recovery of Israel’s borders (2 Kings 14:25). Their story. God sent him to preach against Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, Israel’s cruel enemy. Instead he took a ship the other way, to Tarshish. In a great storm the sailors threw him overboard, and God appointed a great fish to swallow him; after three days and three nights he prayed, and the fish brought him to land (Jonah 1–2). He then preached, and the whole city, from the king down, repented, and God spared it (Jonah 3). Jonah was angry, because he had known God would be merciful. God taught him through a plant that grew and withered (Jonah 4). Remember. Jonah shows that salvation belongs to the LORD and that his mercy is wider than our prejudices. Jesus called his own death and resurrection “the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39–41). Jonah 2:9 Salvation belongs to the LORD! The heart of Jonah’s prayer from inside the fish. Jonah 4:2 for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster. Jonah’s complaint shows that he knew God’s mercy but did not want it for his enemies. Matthew 12:40 For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Jesus points to Jonah as a sign of his death and resurrection.

Hosea Hosea was a prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel whose marriage to an unfaithful wife pictured God’s love for his unfaithful people. Who. Hosea was the son of Beeri. He prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BC, in the days of Jeroboam II of Israel and Kings Uzziah to Hezekiah of Judah (Hosea 1:1), shortly before Assyria destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. Their story. God told him to marry Gomer, a woman who would be unfaithful to him. Their children were given names that were warnings: Jezreel, No Mercy and Not My People (Hosea 1). Gomer left him, but God told him to love her again, and he bought her back for fifteen shekels of silver and some barley (Hosea 3). His book pleads with Israel to return from idols to the LORD, and speaks of God’s tender, aching love: “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” (Hosea 11:8). Remember. Hosea’s marriage shows the faithfulness of God to faithless people. The New Testament applies his words to the gospel: those who were “not my people” are now called “sons of the living God” (Romans 9:25–26; compare 1 Peter 2:10). Christ is the faithful husband who pays to bring his bride home. Hosea 3:1 Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods Hosea’s love for Gomer pictures God’s love for his people. Hosea 11:8 My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. God’s compassion for his rebellious people.

Amos Amos was a shepherd from Judah whom God sent to warn the rich northern kingdom of Israel about injustice and coming judgment. Who. Amos came from Tekoa, a village south of Bethlehem in Judah. He was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore figs, not a trained prophet (Amos 7:14). He prophesied in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam II king of Israel, “two years before the earthquake” (Amos 1:1), about 760 BC. He is a different man from Amoz, Isaiah’s father. Their story. He began by announcing God’s judgment on the nations around Israel, then turned to Israel itself (Amos 1–2). He condemned the rich for crushing the poor, taking bribes and enjoying luxury, while keeping up busy religious festivals (Amos 4–6). He saw visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit (Amos 7–8). Amaziah, the priest at Bethel, told him to go home, but Amos answered that the LORD had sent him (Amos 7:10–17). The book ends with the promise that God will raise up David’s fallen booth (Amos 9:11–15). Remember. God cares how his people treat the poor; worship without justice is hateful to him. James quoted Amos’s closing promise to show that Gentiles are welcomed in Christ, David’s greater Son (Acts 15:16–17). Amos 5:24 But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. What God wants instead of empty religious feasts. Amos 7:15 But the LORD took me from following the flock Amos’s call came from God, not from his background or training.

Micah Micah was a prophet from the Judean countryside who denounced injustice and foretold that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem. Who. Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the lowlands of Judah. He prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Micah 1:1), about 740–700 BC, at the same time as Isaiah. His name means “Who is like the LORD?” He is not the Micah of Ephraim who made an idol (Judges 17–18), nor Micaiah son of Imlah (1 Kings 22). Their story. He spoke against both Samaria and Jerusalem, condemning landowners who seized fields and houses, false prophets who preached for money, and rulers who hated justice (Micah 2–3). He warned that Jerusalem would become a heap of ruins (Micah 3:12); a century later the elders remembered that Hezekiah had listened and repented (Jeremiah 26:18–19). He promised a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2) and ended praising a God who pardons sin and casts it into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:18–19). Remember. God asks for justice, kindness and a humble walk with him. Where we fail, the ruler from Bethlehem, Jesus, brings the pardon Micah praised (Matthew 2:5–6). Micah 6:8 and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? Micah’s summary of what God wants from his people. Micah 5:2 But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel Quoted by the chief priests when the wise men came looking for the newborn King.

Huldah Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem whom King Josiah consulted when the Book of the Law was found. Who. Huldah lived in Jerusalem, in the part of the city called the Second Quarter, in the reign of King Josiah, about 622 BC. She was the wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, probably in charge of the robes for the temple or the palace (2 Kings 22:14; 2 Chronicles 34:22). She lived at the same time as Jeremiah and Zephaniah. Their story. When the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple and it was read to Josiah, the king tore his clothes and sent his officials to ask the LORD what it meant. They went to Huldah. She declared that every curse written in the book would fall on Jerusalem because the people had forsaken God. But because Josiah had humbled himself, he would be gathered to his grave in peace before the disaster came (2 Kings 22:14–20). Remember. Huldah spoke plainly and faithfully: the written word of God means what it says. She is one of a small number of women the Old Testament calls prophets, and her ministry shows God’s care in speaking to his people, warning them of judgment and giving mercy to the humble. 2 Kings 22:14 So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess The king’s officials seek God’s word through Huldah. 2 Kings 22:19 because your heart was penitent, and you humbled yourself before the LORD Her message of mercy for the humble king.

Ezekiel A priest carried off to Babylon who became God’s prophet to the exiles there. Who. Ezekiel, son of Buzi, was a priest from Jerusalem. He was taken to Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin and lived among the exiles by the Chebar canal. God called him in 593 BC, when he was probably thirty years old, and he prophesied for about twenty-two years. God addresses him over ninety times as “son of man”, meaning simply a frail human being. He is the only Ezekiel in the Bible. Their story. He saw the glory of God on a throne above living creatures and wheels (Ezekiel 1–3). He acted out signs of Jerusalem’s coming siege and saw God’s glory leave the defiled temple (Ezekiel 4–11). When his wife died, God told him not to mourn openly, as a sign of the grief to come (Ezekiel 24:15–27). After news came that Jerusalem had fallen in 586 BC, his message turned to hope: God himself would shepherd his flock, give a new heart, raise dry bones to life and dwell in a new temple (Ezekiel 33–48). Remember. Ezekiel teaches that God judges sin, yet does not abandon his people. The promised good shepherd is Jesus (John 10:11), and the new heart comes by his Spirit. Ezekiel 1:3 the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there. God met his people in exile, far from the temple, through this priest. Ezekiel 36:26 And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. The heart of Ezekiel’s hope: God himself will change his people from within. Ezekiel shows that God’s glory is not tied to one building, and that he can bring dead hearts to life.

Daniel A young man of Judah taken to Babylon who served foreign kings faithfully and received visions of God’s kingdom. Who. Daniel came from a noble family of Judah and was taken to Babylon as a youth in 605 BC. There he was renamed Belteshazzar and trained for royal service. He lived through the whole exile, serving until at least the third year of Cyrus, about 536 BC (Daniel 10:1). Do not confuse him with David’s son Daniel (1 Chronicles 3:1) or the priest Daniel who returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:2). Their story. He refused the king’s food rather than defile himself, and God gave him wisdom (Daniel 1). He told and explained Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a great statue broken by a stone (Daniel 2), and later read the writing on the wall for Belshazzar (Daniel 5). Under Darius the Mede he kept praying to God against the law and was thrown to the lions, but God shut their mouths (Daniel 6). His visions show the kingdoms of the world giving way to the everlasting kingdom of “one like a son of man” (Daniel 7–12). Remember. Scripture records no great fall in Daniel’s life, yet he confessed “we have sinned” with his people (Daniel 9:5). Jesus took the title Son of Man from Daniel 7, and his kingdom is the one that will never end. Daniel 1:8 But Daniel resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food, or with the wine that he drank. Daniel’s faithfulness began with a quiet decision when he was young. Daniel 6:10 He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously. Daniel did not change his habit of prayer when it became dangerous. Daniel 2:44 And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed Behind all the empires stands the kingdom of God, which outlasts them all. Daniel shows how to live faithfully as a believer in a culture that does not honour God.

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego Three young Jews in Babylon who would not bow to a golden statue and were saved from the fiery furnace. Who. Their Hebrew names were Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah; the chief of the eunuchs gave them Babylonian names (Daniel 1:6–7). They were friends of Daniel, taken from Judah to Babylon in about 605 BC and trained for the king’s service. They should not be confused with the many other men in the Old Testament called Hananiah or Azariah. Their story. With Daniel they refused the king’s food and were found ten times wiser than the king’s wise men (Daniel 1). They prayed with Daniel for God to reveal the king’s dream, and afterwards were made officials over the province of Babylon (Daniel 2:17–18, 49). When Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image about 90 feet (27 m) high and commanded all to worship it, they refused. Thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter, they walked unharmed in the fire with a fourth figure (Daniel 3). Nebuchadnezzar said God had sent his angel; many Christians have believed it was the Son of God himself, before he became man. Remember. Their faith did not depend on being rescued: “But if not”. God did not keep them from the fire, but he was with them in it, as he promises to be with his people (Isaiah 43:2). Daniel 3:17 If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. They trusted that God was able to save them. Daniel 3:18 But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up. Even if God chose not to rescue them, they would still not worship an idol. Daniel 3:25 But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt God was present with his servants in the furnace.

Nebuchadnezzar The king of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem and was humbled by the God of Israel. Who. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon from 605 to 562 BC. He took Daniel, Ezekiel and many others into exile and burned Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC. For his reign, his wars and his place in history, see the Nebuchadnezzar card in The Bible’s World. This card looks at him as a person in the Bible’s story. Their story. He dreamed of a great statue and learned from Daniel that God gives kingdoms to whom he wills (Daniel 2). He set up a golden image and threw Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego into the furnace, then praised their God when they were saved (Daniel 3). Boasting over the greatness of Babylon, he was struck with madness and lived like an animal until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (Daniel 4). Jeremiah calls him God’s “servant”, the tool God used to judge Judah (Jeremiah 25:9). Remember. Nebuchadnezzar was cruel and proud, yet God humbled him and brought him to praise the King of heaven. Scholars differ on whether he truly came to saving faith. His story shows that no ruler is beyond God’s reach. Daniel 4:30 Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty? The proud boast that came just before God humbled him. Daniel 4:37 Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble. The humbled king confessed that God rules over all.

Belshazzar The last ruler of Babylon, who saw the writing on the wall the night the city fell. Who. Belshazzar was the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon. For years his father lived away from the city, and Belshazzar ruled Babylon in his place. That is probably why he could offer Daniel only the third place in the kingdom (Daniel 5:16). Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar his “father”, which in that world could mean ancestor or royal predecessor. Daniel also dates two visions by his reign (Daniel 7:1; 8:1). Their story. In 539 BC, while the Persian army was outside the walls, Belshazzar held a great feast. He drank wine from the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem and praised idols. A hand appeared and wrote on the wall MENE, MENE, TEKEL and PARSIN. Daniel explained that God had numbered his kingdom, weighed him and found him wanting, and given his kingdom to the Medes and Persians. That very night Belshazzar was killed and Babylon fell (Daniel 5). Remember. Belshazzar knew how God had humbled Nebuchadnezzar, yet he did not humble his own heart (Daniel 5:22). His story warns against mocking what belongs to God, and reminds us that every life will be weighed. Only those clothed in Christ’s righteousness will not be found wanting. Daniel 5:23 but you have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven. Daniel names Belshazzar’s real sin: pride against God. Daniel 5:27 TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; God’s verdict on a life lived without honouring him. Daniel 5:30 That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed. God’s judgment came swiftly, on the night of his feast.

Esther A Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia and risked her life to save her people. Who. Esther, also called Hadassah, was a Jewish girl of the tribe of Benjamin living in Susa, a capital of Persia. Her parents had died, and her older cousin Mordecai raised her as his daughter (Esther 2:7). She became queen to King Ahasuerus, usually identified as Xerxes I (486 to 465 BC), in about 479 BC. Their story. When Queen Vashti was removed, Esther was taken into the king’s harem and chosen as queen; on Mordecai’s advice she kept her Jewish identity hidden (Esther 1–2). Haman then won a decree to destroy all the Jews. Mordecai urged Esther to plead with the king, though coming to him unsummoned could mean death. After three days of fasting she went in, and the king held out his golden sceptre (Esther 3–5). At her second banquet she exposed Haman’s plot (Esther 7). A new decree let the Jews defend themselves, and the feast of Purim was set up to remember their rescue (Esther 8–9). Remember. God’s name is never mentioned in Esther, yet his hidden hand rules every turn. Esther was no flawless heroine; she hid her faith and lived in a pagan court. Yet God used her. She risked her life to plead for her people; Christ gave his life and now pleads for his. Esther 4:14 And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this? Mordecai saw God’s purpose in Esther’s position. Esther 4:16 Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish. Esther’s courageous resolve to stand between her people and death. Esther shows that God is at work for his people even when he seems silent.

Mordecai The Jewish cousin and guardian of Queen Esther, who refused to bow to Haman and rose to high office in Persia. Who. Mordecai was a Benjamite, the son of Jair, living in Susa in the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I), about 480 BC. His family had been carried into exile from Jerusalem (Esther 2:5–6). He raised his orphaned cousin Esther and seems to have held an official post at the king’s gate. He is not the Mordecai who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2). Their story. Mordecai uncovered a plot by two officials to kill the king, and it was written in the royal records (Esther 2:21–23). He refused to bow down to Haman, which provoked Haman to plot against all the Jews (Esther 3). He urged Esther to go to the king (Esther 4). On a sleepless night the king read of Mordecai’s good deed, and Haman was made to lead him through the city in royal honour (Esther 6). After Haman’s fall Mordecai received the king’s signet ring and became second only to the king (Esther 8:2; 10:3). Remember. Mordecai was faithful and courageous, and he used his power for the good of his people. His sudden rise from danger to honour shows how God raises the humble and brings down the proud. Esther 3:5 And when Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury. Mordecai’s refusal to bow set the whole story in motion. Esther 10:3 For Mordecai the Jew was second in rank to King Ahasuerus, and he was great among the Jews and popular with the multitude of his brothers, for he sought the welfare of his people and spoke peace to all his people. Mordecai used his high position to seek his people’s good.

Haman The proud Persian official who plotted to destroy all the Jews and was hanged on his own gallows. Who. Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, was the chief official of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) in about 474 BC (Esther 3:1, 7). “Agagite” probably links him to Agag, king of the Amalekites, Israel’s ancient enemies (1 Samuel 15). His wife was Zeresh, and he had ten sons (Esther 5:10; 9:10). Their story. When Mordecai would not bow to him, Haman set out to destroy all the Jews in the empire. He cast lots, called pur, to choose the day, and persuaded the king to issue the decree (Esther 3). He built a gallows fifty cubits, about 75 feet (23 m), high for Mordecai (Esther 5:14). But the king, unable to sleep, decided to honour Mordecai, and Haman had to lead him through the city (Esther 6). At Esther’s banquet his plot was exposed, and he was hanged on the gallows he had built (Esther 7). The feast of Purim takes its name from his lots (Esther 9:24–26). Remember. Haman shows that pride and hatred destroy the one who holds them. God turned his plan upside down, as at the cross he turned the worst evil into the salvation of his people. Esther 3:6 Haman sought to destroy all the Jews, the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus. Wounded pride grew into a plan for mass murder. Esther 7:10 So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. The trap Haman set for another caught himself. Proverbs 16:18 Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. Haman’s life is a living example of this proverb.

Zerubbabel The governor of Judah from David’s royal line who led the return from Babylon and rebuilt the temple. Who. Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin and so an heir of David. He is usually called the son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2), though 1 Chronicles 3:19 names Pedaiah as his father; scholars differ on how to fit these together. The Persians made him governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1). He is listed in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:12–13). Their story. In about 538 BC he led the first large group of exiles home with Joshua the high priest (Ezra 2:2). They rebuilt the altar and laid the temple foundation, but local enemies opposed them and the work stopped for about sixteen years (Ezra 3–4). In 520 BC the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stirred him to start again, and the temple was finished in 516 BC (Ezra 5–6). God told him that the work would succeed “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”, and called him his chosen signet ring (Zechariah 4:6; Haggai 2:23). Remember. Zerubbabel never sat on David’s throne, yet God kept David’s line alive through him. The promise he carried came true in Jesus, the true King, who builds God’s lasting temple, his people. Ezra 3:2 Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel The returned exiles began by restoring the worship of God. Zechariah 4:6 This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts. The rebuilding depended on God’s Spirit, not human strength. Haggai 2:23 I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you God renewed his promise to David’s line through Zerubbabel.

Joshua the high priest The high priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and led the rebuilding of the temple’s worship. Who. Joshua, son of Jehozadak, is called Jeshua in Ezra and Nehemiah. His grandfather Seraiah was the high priest put to death by Nebuchadnezzar, and his father went into exile (1 Chronicles 6:14–15). He returned to Jerusalem in about 538 BC. Do not confuse him with Joshua son of Nun, who led Israel into Canaan. His name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus. Their story. With Zerubbabel he rebuilt the altar, restored the sacrifices and laid the temple foundation (Ezra 3). When the work restarted in 520 BC he took part again (Haggai 1:12–14; Ezra 5:2). In a vision Zechariah saw him in filthy clothes, accused by Satan; the Lord rebuked Satan, and Joshua was given clean garments as a sign that his sin was taken away (Zechariah 3). Later Zechariah was told to set a crown on his head, as a sign of the coming Branch who would be both priest and king (Zechariah 6:9–15). Some of his descendants later married foreign wives (Ezra 10:18). Remember. Joshua could not stand before God in his own clothes. His cleansing pictures the gospel: Jesus, the true High Priest and King, removes our sin and clothes us in his righteousness. Zechariah 3:1 Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. Even the high priest needed God’s mercy against the accuser. Zechariah 3:4 Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments. God himself takes away sin and gives clean clothing. Zechariah 6:12 Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: for he shall branch out from his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD. Joshua’s crowning pointed ahead to the Messiah.

Haggai The prophet who urged the returned exiles in 520 BC to finish rebuilding the temple. Who. Haggai prophesied in Jerusalem in 520 BC, in the second year of Darius I of Persia. All four of his messages fall within about four months. The Bible tells us nothing about his family; Ezra names him with Zechariah as the prophets who encouraged the builders (Ezra 5:1; 6:14). He is the only Haggai in Scripture. Their story. The temple had lain unfinished for about sixteen years while the people built their own houses. Haggai told them that their poor harvests were God’s discipline for neglecting his house (Haggai 1:1–11). Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people obeyed and began work within weeks (Haggai 1:12–15). When older people wept that the new temple was nothing like Solomon’s, Haggai promised that God would shake the nations and that its latter glory would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:1–9). He reminded them that holy work does not make unholy people clean (Haggai 2:10–19), and ended with God’s promise to Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:20–23). Remember. Haggai calls God’s people to put him first. The greater glory he promised came when Jesus himself walked in that temple (John 2:19–21). Haggai 1:4 Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? Haggai challenged misplaced priorities. Haggai 1:13 Then Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, spoke to the people with the LORD’s message, “I am with you, declares the LORD.” God’s presence was the people’s encouragement to work. Haggai 2:9 The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. A promise fulfilled when Christ came to the temple.

Zechariah the prophet The prophet who encouraged the returned exiles with visions of God’s plans and promises of the coming King. Who. Zechariah was the son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo (Zechariah 1:1); Ezra calls him “son of Iddo”, meaning his descendant (Ezra 5:1). He came from a priestly family that returned from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:4, 16). He began to prophesy in 520 BC, two months after Haggai. About thirty men in the Bible are called Zechariah, among them the priest stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22) and the father of John the Baptist (Luke 1). Their story. In eight night visions he saw horsemen, a lampstand, a flying scroll and the high priest Joshua cleansed, all assuring the people that God would restore Jerusalem and finish the temple (Zechariah 1–6). He called them to true justice and mercy rather than empty fasting (Zechariah 7–8). His later prophecies speak of a humble king riding on a donkey, a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver, one who is pierced and a shepherd struck down (Zechariah 9–14). Remember. Zechariah’s name means “the LORD remembers”. The gospels show that his prophecies of the King came true in Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem, betrayal and death (Matthew 21:5; John 19:37). Zechariah 1:1 In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo His ministry is dated precisely to 520 BC. Zechariah 9:9 Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. Fulfilled when Jesus entered Jerusalem on Palm Sunday. Zechariah 12:10 when they look on me, on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only child John sees this fulfilled at the cross.

Ezra A priest and scribe who led exiles back from Babylon and taught God’s law to the people in Jerusalem. Who. Ezra was a priest descended from Aaron and a scribe, that is, a scholar and teacher of the Law of Moses (Ezra 7:1–6). He came to Jerusalem in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes I, probably 458 BC, about eighty years after the first return. He later worked alongside Nehemiah. Their story. With the king’s letter and gifts for the temple, Ezra led some 1,500 men and their families from Babylon. Ashamed to ask for soldiers after telling the king that God protects his people, he fasted and prayed, and they arrived safely after about four months (Ezra 7–8). Finding that many, even priests and leaders, had married women who worshipped other gods, he tore his clothes, confessed the people’s sin as his own, and led them to put things right (Ezra 9–10). Years later he read the Law aloud to the gathered people from morning until midday, while the Levites explained it, and the people wept and then rejoiced (Nehemiah 8). Remember. Ezra shows the value of a life given to studying, obeying and teaching God’s word, in that order. His prayer of confession shows a leader who stood with sinful people rather than above them. Ezra 7:10 For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel. The pattern of Ezra’s life: study, practice, then teaching. Ezra 9:6 O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads Ezra confessed his people’s sin as if it were his own. Nehemiah 8:8 They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading. God’s word was read and explained so that ordinary people could understand.

Nehemiah The Jewish cupbearer to the Persian king who became governor of Judah and rebuilt Jerusalem’s walls. Who. Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah, was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes I at Susa, a trusted post that meant tasting and serving the king’s wine. In 445 BC he heard that Jerusalem’s walls lay in ruins. He served as governor of Judah for twelve years and then returned for a second term. Do not confuse him with the Nehemiah who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2). Their story. He wept, fasted and prayed for months, then asked the king to send him to rebuild the city (Nehemiah 1–2). He organised the people by families, and despite mockery and threats from Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, they finished the wall in fifty-two days, working with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other (Nehemiah 3–6). He stopped the rich from enslaving poorer Jews and refused a governor’s allowance (Nehemiah 5). With Ezra he led the reading of the Law and the renewal of the covenant (Nehemiah 8–10). On his return he cleansed the temple and enforced the Sabbath, sometimes with harsh anger (Nehemiah 13). Remember. Nehemiah joined prayer with hard work. Yet his book ends with the people already slipping back, showing that walls and reforms cannot change hearts. Only Christ can. Nehemiah 1:4 As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven. Nehemiah’s work began with grief and prayer. Nehemiah 4:14 Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes. He steadied frightened builders by turning their eyes to God. Nehemiah 6:3 I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. He would not be distracted from the task God had given him.

Malachi The last of the Old Testament prophets, who called God’s people back from careless worship and promised the coming messenger. Who. Malachi’s name means “my messenger”, and some think it may be a title rather than a personal name; scholars differ. Nothing is known of his family. He probably prophesied in Jerusalem around the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, about 460 to 430 BC, when the temple was rebuilt but the people’s devotion had grown cold. Their story. His book is set out as a series of arguments: God speaks, the people question him, and God answers. He rebuked priests who offered blind and lame animals (Malachi 1), men who broke faith with their wives by divorce (Malachi 2), and a people who robbed God by holding back tithes (Malachi 3:8–10). He promised that God would send his messenger to prepare the way, and then the Lord himself would come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). He ended by promising Elijah before the great day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5–6). After him no prophet spoke for about four hundred years. Remember. Malachi shows that God’s love remains even when his people’s worship grows dull. Jesus said John the Baptist was the promised messenger and Elijah (Matthew 11:10, 14), so Malachi opens the door to the gospel. Malachi 3:1 Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple Fulfilled in John the Baptist and in the coming of Jesus. Malachi 4:2 But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings. A promise of healing and joy for those who fear God. Malachi 4:5 Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. The Old Testament closes looking for this promised forerunner.

Mary the mother of Jesus The young Jewish woman of Nazareth chosen by God to be the virgin mother of Jesus. Who. Mary was a young woman of Nazareth in Galilee, engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David. Jesus was born to her about 6 to 4 BC. She is called “Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14) to tell her apart from the several other Marys of the Gospels. After Jesus she had other children with Joseph, among them James and Jude (Mark 6:3). Their story. The angel Gabriel told her she would conceive by the Holy Spirit, and she humbly accepted God’s word (Luke 1:26–38). She visited Elizabeth and sang the song known as the Magnificat (Luke 1:39–56). She gave birth in Bethlehem and pondered all that happened (Luke 2). At the wedding at Cana she told the servants, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). For a time she and Jesus’ brothers did not understand his work (Mark 3:21, 31–35). She stood by the cross, where Jesus gave her into John’s care (John 19:25–27), and she prayed with the disciples after the ascension (Acts 1:14). Remember. Mary is a model of humble faith. She called God “my Saviour” (Luke 1:47): she too needed the salvation her Son brought. We honour her as blessed, but we do not pray to her; our hope is in her Son alone. Luke 1:38 And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” Mary’s faith: a simple, willing trust in what God has said. Luke 2:19 But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart. She thought deeply about what God was doing through her child. Mary shows that God chooses the lowly and that the right answer to his word is trusting obedience.

Joseph of Nazareth The carpenter of Nazareth, descended from David, who married Mary and raised Jesus as his own son. Who. Joseph was a builder or carpenter (Matthew 13:55) from the royal line of David, living in Nazareth. He was engaged to Mary and became the legal father of Jesus, though not his natural father. Do not confuse him with Joseph the son of Jacob in Genesis, or with Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Jesus. Their story. When he found Mary was pregnant, he planned to end the engagement quietly, but an angel told him in a dream that the child was from the Holy Spirit; he obeyed and took Mary as his wife (Matthew 1:18–25). He took his family to Bethlehem for the census, where Jesus was born (Luke 2:1–7). Warned in dreams, he fled with them to Egypt and later settled in Nazareth (Matthew 2:13–23). He took twelve-year-old Jesus to the temple at Passover (Luke 2:41–51). He is not mentioned after this and had probably died before Jesus’ public ministry began. Remember. Joseph was a quiet man of quick obedience. Through him Jesus was legally the son of David, heir to David’s throne, as God had promised. Matthew 1:19 And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. Even before he understood, Joseph was both righteous and merciful. Matthew 1:24 When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, He obeyed God at once, at real cost to his reputation.

Zechariah and Elizabeth An elderly priest and his wife who, after long childlessness, became the parents of John the Baptist. Who. Zechariah was a priest of the division of Abijah, and his wife Elizabeth was also from a priestly family, descended from Aaron. They lived in the hill country of Judea. Elizabeth was a relative of Mary, Jesus’ mother. Do not confuse this Zechariah with the Old Testament prophet Zechariah, or with the Zechariah murdered in the temple (Matthew 23:35). Their story. They were righteous but childless and old (Luke 1:5–7). While Zechariah burned incense in the temple, the angel Gabriel told him Elizabeth would bear a son to be named John. He doubted, so he was made unable to speak until the birth (Luke 1:8–25). When Mary visited, Elizabeth’s baby leapt in her womb, and, filled with the Spirit, she called Mary “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:39–45). At John’s naming Zechariah wrote “His name is John,” found his voice again, and sang a song of praise known as the Benedictus (Luke 1:57–79). Remember. God keeps his promises in his own time, even when his servants doubt. Zechariah’s song praises God for sending the Saviour, of whom their son would be the forerunner. Luke 1:6 And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. Their faithfulness was real, even though their prayers for a child seemed unanswered. Luke 1:13 But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. God had heard their long-standing prayer. Luke 1:68 “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people Zechariah’s first words are praise for the coming redemption.

John the Baptist The prophet sent ahead of Jesus to prepare the way by calling Israel to repent and be baptized. Who. John was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, born about six months before Jesus. He lived in the wilderness, wore camel’s hair and ate locusts and wild honey, like the prophet Elijah (Matthew 3:4). He is called “the Baptist” (the baptizer) to tell him apart from John the apostle, the son of Zebedee. Their story. He preached repentance and baptized people in the Jordan, as the voice in the wilderness foretold by Isaiah (Matthew 3:1–12). He baptized Jesus and saw the Spirit descend on him (Matthew 3:13–17). He pointed his own disciples to Jesus as the Lamb of God (John 1:29–37). When he rebuked Herod Antipas for marrying his brother’s wife, he was imprisoned, and there he sent to ask whether Jesus was the one to come (Matthew 11:2–6). Herod had him beheaded, about AD 29 to 32 (Mark 6:14–29). Remember. John’s whole life pointed away from himself to Christ. Jesus called him the greatest born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater, for they see the finished work John only foretold. John 1:29 The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! John’s great message: Jesus is the sacrifice for sin. John 3:30 He must increase, but I must decrease. The heart of John’s humility and of every true ministry. Matthew 11:11 Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. Jesus’ verdict on John, and on the privilege of living after the cross.

Simeon A devout old man in Jerusalem who took the baby Jesus in his arms and praised God for his salvation. Who. Simeon lived in Jerusalem when Jesus was born. Luke calls him righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation (comfort) of Israel. The Holy Spirit had shown him he would not die before he saw the Lord’s Christ. He is often pictured as old, though Luke does not give his age. Do not confuse him with Simeon the son of Jacob, or with Simon Peter. Their story. Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple when Mary and Joseph brought the forty-day-old Jesus to present him to the Lord (Luke 2:22–27). He took the child in his arms and blessed God in the song known as the Nunc Dimittis: now he could depart in peace, for he had seen God’s salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel (Luke 2:28–32). He warned Mary that the child would cause the fall and rising of many, and that a sword would pierce her own soul (Luke 2:34–35). Remember. Simeon waited patiently on God’s promise and saw it kept. To see Jesus is to see God’s salvation, for Jews and Gentiles alike. Luke 2:25 Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. A picture of faithful waiting on God’s promises. Luke 2:30 for my eyes have seen your salvation Salvation is not an idea but a person, the child in his arms.

Anna An aged prophetess who served God in the temple and spoke about the infant Jesus to all who longed for redemption. Who. Anna was the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had been married for seven years and then lived as a widow, probably to the age of eighty-four (some read it as eighty-four years of widowhood). She never left the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. She is the only Anna in the Bible. Their story. She came up at the very hour Simeon was blessing the baby Jesus in the temple. She gave thanks to God and spoke about the child to everyone who was waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38). Remember. Anna shows that a long life of hidden prayer is not wasted. God let this faithful widow see the Redeemer, and her first response was thanksgiving and telling others about him. Luke 2:36 And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. Luke carefully records her family and tribe; she was a real, known woman. Luke 2:38 And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. Thanksgiving and witness are the natural fruit of seeing Christ. Anna is a model of patient, prayerful faith in old age.

Peter (Simon) A Galilean fisherman who became the leading apostle of Jesus, denied him, was restored and led the early church. Who. Simon, son of John (or Jonah), was a fisherman from Bethsaida living at Capernaum, and was married (Mark 1:30). His brother was Andrew. Jesus named him Cephas (Aramaic) or Peter (Greek), both meaning “rock”. He is listed first among the twelve. Do not confuse him with Simon the Zealot, another apostle. Their story. Andrew brought him to Jesus (John 1:40–42), and he left his nets to follow (Luke 5:1–11). He walked briefly on water and then began to sink (Matthew 14:28–31). He confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, then rebuked Jesus for speaking of the cross (Matthew 16:13–23). He saw the transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8). He boasted he would never fall away, yet denied Jesus three times and wept bitterly (Luke 22:31–62). The risen Lord restored him three times over (John 21:15–19). He preached at Pentecost and led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 2–12), and he wrote 1 and 2 Peter. Early tradition says he was crucified in Rome, about AD 64 to 68. Remember. Peter is proof that Christ restores failed disciples. His strength was never his own; the rock the church is built on is the truth he confessed about Jesus. Matthew 16:16 Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The great confession on which the church stands. Luke 22:62 And he went out and wept bitterly. The bitterness of his denial was the start of true repentance. John 21:17 He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep. Three denials are met by three gentle questions and a new commission.

Andrew A fisherman of Galilee, brother of Peter, and one of the first disciples to follow Jesus. Who. Andrew was the son of John and brother of Simon Peter, from Bethsaida, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. He was one of the twelve apostles. His name is Greek, meaning “manly”. He is the only Andrew in the Bible. Their story. He was first a disciple of John the Baptist, and followed Jesus when John called him the Lamb of God (John 1:35–40).
