He at once found his brother Simon and brought him to Jesus (John 1:41–42). Later Jesus called the two brothers from their nets to be fishers of men (Mark 1:16–18). At the feeding of the five thousand he brought the boy with five loaves and two fish (John 6:8–9), and with Philip he brought some Greeks who wanted to see Jesus (John 12:20–22). He was among those who asked Jesus about the end of the age (Mark 13:3). Later traditions about his death are uncertain. Remember. Andrew is remembered for bringing people to Jesus. He was less prominent than his brother, but his quiet witness began Peter’s story. John 1:40 One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. Andrew was one of the very first to follow Jesus. John 1:41 He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ). His first act as a disciple was to bring his brother.

James son of Zebedee A Galilean fisherman, brother of John, one of Jesus’ closest apostles and the first of the twelve to be martyred. Who. James was the son of Zebedee, a fisherman, and probably of Salome. He and his brother John were partners with Peter. Jesus called the brothers “Boanerges”, meaning Sons of Thunder, probably for their fiery temper. He is sometimes called James the Great. Do not confuse him with James son of Alphaeus (another apostle) or James the brother of Jesus, who led the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James. Their story. He left his father’s boat to follow Jesus (Mark 1:19–20). With Peter and John he saw Jairus’ daughter raised, the transfiguration and Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 14:33). He and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54) and asked for the best seats in the kingdom (Mark 10:35–45). Herod Agrippa I had him killed with the sword, about AD 44 (Acts 12:1–2). Remember. James asked for glory and Jesus promised him his cup of suffering instead. He drank it faithfully, the first apostle to die for Christ. Mark 3:17 James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Jesus named the brothers for their zeal. Acts 12:2 He killed James the brother of John with the sword. Jesus’ words that James would share his cup came true (Mark 10:39).

John son of Zebedee A Galilean fisherman, brother of James, who became one of Jesus’ closest apostles and wrote the Gospel of John. Who. John was the son of Zebedee and the younger brother of James. He is traditionally understood to be “the disciple whom Jesus loved” in the Fourth Gospel. The church has long held that he wrote John’s Gospel, three letters and Revelation. Do not confuse him with John the Baptist or with John Mark, who wrote Mark’s Gospel. Their story. He left his nets to follow Jesus (Mark 1:19–20) and was one of the inner three with Peter and James (Mark 9:2). He once tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name (Mark 9:38) and wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). He leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13:23), stood by the cross, and was given care of Mary (John 19:26–27). He ran to the empty tomb (John 20:2–8). With Peter he preached in Jerusalem and was imprisoned (Acts 3–4). Later he was exiled on Patmos (Revelation 1:9), and tradition says he died old, in Ephesus, about AD 100. Remember. The hot-tempered Son of Thunder became the apostle of love. Christ’s love changes those it lays hold of. John 13:23 One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side, John found his identity in being loved by Jesus. John 21:24 This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true. The Gospel of John rests on an eyewitness.

Matthew (Levi) A tax collector at Capernaum whom Jesus called to be an apostle, and the writer of the first Gospel. Who. Matthew, also called Levi the son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14), collected taxes and tolls at Capernaum for Herod Antipas. Tax collectors were despised as greedy and as collaborators with foreign rulers. He was one of the twelve. The church has always held that he wrote the Gospel of Matthew. His father Alphaeus is probably not the same man as the father of James son of Alphaeus, though some think so. Their story. Jesus saw him at his tax booth and said, “Follow me,” and he rose and followed (Matthew 9:9). He held a great feast in his house for Jesus with many tax collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees complained (Luke 5:27–32). Jesus answered that he came to call sinners to repentance. In his own Gospel’s list of apostles, he calls himself “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3). Remember. Matthew never forgot what he had been. Jesus calls sinners, not the self-righteous, and the grace that found Matthew at his tax booth can find anyone. Matthew 9:9 As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. A swift, costly response to Jesus’ call. Matthew’s story shows that no one is beyond the reach of Christ’s call.

Thomas One of the twelve apostles, remembered for doubting the resurrection and then confessing Jesus as Lord and God. Who. Thomas was one of the twelve. His name means “twin” in Aramaic, and John also gives his Greek name, Didymus, with the same meaning (John 11:16). We are not told who his twin was. Nothing is known of his family or earlier work. Their story. When Jesus set out for Judea, where his life was in danger, Thomas said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16). At the Last Supper he asked, “How can we know the way?” and Jesus answered, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:5–6). He was absent when the risen Jesus first appeared to the disciples, and would not believe without touching his wounds. A week later Jesus appeared and invited him to touch; Thomas confessed, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:24–29). He was among those fishing when Jesus appeared by the sea (John 21:2). Later tradition says he took the gospel to India. Remember. Thomas was loyal but slow to believe. Jesus met his doubt with patience, and his confession is one of the clearest in Scripture that Jesus is God. John 11:16 So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.” Thomas was gloomy but loyal. John 20:28 Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” The doubter makes the Gospel’s highest confession of who Jesus is.

Philip the apostle One of the twelve apostles, from Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus. Who. Philip came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). His name is Greek. He was one of the twelve and is mostly known from John’s Gospel. Do not confuse him with Philip the evangelist, one of the seven chosen in Acts 6, who preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian (Acts 8), or with Herod Philip. Their story. Jesus found him and said, “Follow me” (John 1:43). He at once found Nathanael and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about; when Nathanael doubted, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:45–46). Before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus tested him by asking where to buy bread, and Philip said two hundred denarii (about eight months’ wages) would not be enough (John 6:5–7). With Andrew he brought Greeks who wished to see Jesus (John 12:20–22). At the Last Supper he asked Jesus to show them the Father (John 14:8–9). Remember. Philip was slow to see, yet Jesus patiently taught him that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father. John 1:43 He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.” Jesus himself sought out Philip. John 14:8 Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” His request led to Jesus’ great answer: to see Jesus is to see the Father.

Bartholomew (Nathanael) One of the twelve apostles, probably the same man as Nathanael of Cana whom Philip brought to Jesus. Who. Bartholomew appears only in the lists of the twelve, always next to Philip (Matthew 10:3). Bartholomew means “son of Tolmai”, a family name. John never uses it but tells of Nathanael, from Cana in Galilee (John 21:2), whom Philip brought to Jesus. Many since early times think they are the same man, though this is not certain. Their story. When Philip told him they had found the Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth, Nathanael asked, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip replied, “Come and see.” Jesus greeted him as an Israelite in whom there was no deceit, and told him he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael confessed, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus promised he would see greater things: heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man (John 1:45–51). He was among the seven who met the risen Jesus by the Sea of Galilee (John 21:2). Remember. Honest doubt, brought to Jesus, can become wholehearted faith. Jesus is the true ladder between heaven and earth, as in Jacob’s dream. John 1:46 Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.” Prejudice answered by an invitation to meet Jesus. John 1:47 Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!” Jesus knew Nathanael’s heart before they met.

Judas Iscariot The apostle who betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. Who. Judas was the son of Simon Iscariot (John 6:71). Iscariot probably means “man of Kerioth”, a town in Judea, which would make him the only one of the twelve not from Galilee. He kept the disciples’ common purse. Do not confuse him with the faithful apostle Judas son of James (also called Thaddaeus), or with Judas (Jude) the brother of Jesus. Their story. He was chosen as one of the twelve (Mark 3:19), yet he stole from the moneybag (John 12:6). He agreed with the chief priests to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14–16), fulfilling Zechariah 11:12–13. At the Last Supper Jesus revealed that one of them would betray him, and Satan entered Judas (John 13:21–30). He led soldiers to Gethsemane and identified Jesus with a kiss (Matthew 26:47–50). Afterwards, filled with remorse, he returned the money and hanged himself (Matthew 27:3–5; Acts 1:18). Matthias took his place among the twelve (Acts 1:26). Remember. Judas was close to Jesus for three years and still was lost. Remorse is not repentance: Peter wept and returned to Christ, but Judas turned away. Yet God used even this betrayal to bring about the cross. Matthew 26:15 and said, “What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?” And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. He sold his Master for the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32). John 12:6 He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it. Love of money had long been at work in him. Matthew 27:3 Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, Regret without turning to Christ could not save him.

The twelve apostles The twelve men Jesus chose to be with him, to be sent out to preach, and to be his witnesses. Who. An apostle is “one who is sent”. The twelve match the twelve tribes of Israel, a sign that Jesus was gathering God’s people anew. Their names: Simon Peter; Andrew his brother; James and John, sons of Zebedee; Philip; Bartholomew; Thomas; Matthew; James son of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot; Judas Iscariot (Matthew 10:2–4). Telling them apart: there are two Jameses (son of Zebedee, and son of Alphaeus, perhaps “James the younger”, Mark 15:40); two Simons (Peter, and Simon the Zealot, also called the Cananaean); and two Judases (Judas Iscariot, and Judas son of James, who is Thaddaeus, Luke 6:16; John 14:22). Their story. Jesus chose them after a night of prayer (Luke 6:12–16). He sent them to preach and heal (Matthew 10). They all deserted him at his arrest (Mark 14:50), but the risen Jesus restored and commissioned them (Matthew 28:16–20). Matthias replaced Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:15–26). Paul was later called as an apostle too (1 Corinthians 15:8–9). Remember. They were ordinary, flawed men. The church is built on their witness to Christ, the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Mark 3:14 And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach First to be with Jesus, then to be sent. Matthew 10:2 The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; The list begins with the two pairs of fishermen brothers. Luke 6:16 and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. Luke carefully distinguishes the two Judases.

Mary Magdalene A woman from whom Jesus drove out seven demons, who followed him and was the first to see him risen. Who. Mary came from Magdala, a town on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee; that is why she is called Magdalene. Jesus had freed her from seven demons. She is not the sinful woman of Luke 7, nor Mary of Bethany; that idea arose centuries later and has no basis in the Gospels. Their story. She travelled with Jesus and the twelve and, with other women, supported them from her own means (Luke 8:1–3). She stood near the cross (John 19:25) and watched where Jesus was buried (Mark 15:47). Early on the first day of the week she came to the tomb and found it empty (John 20:1–2). Weeping outside, she met the risen Jesus but did not know him until he called her by name; she then told the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” (John 20:11–18). Remember. Mary’s devotion was the response of someone set free. The first witness to the resurrection was a woman once enslaved by demons, which shows the grace of the risen Christ. Luke 8:2 and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, What Jesus had done for her explains her love for him. John 20:16 Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher). The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). John 20:18 Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord” She becomes the first messenger of the resurrection.

Mary and Martha of Bethany Two sisters of Bethany near Jerusalem, close friends of Jesus, whose brother was Lazarus. Who. Martha and Mary lived with their brother Lazarus in Bethany, a village about two miles (3 km) from Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives. Jesus loved all three (John 11:5). This Mary is not Mary Magdalene, nor the sinful woman who anointed Jesus in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50). Their story. Martha welcomed Jesus into her home but was distracted with much serving, while Mary sat at his feet listening. Jesus told Martha that Mary had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42). When Lazarus died, Martha went to meet Jesus and confessed him as the Christ, the Son of God; Mary fell weeping at his feet, and Jesus wept with them before raising Lazarus (John 11:17–44). Six days before the Passover, at a supper in Bethany, Martha served and Mary anointed Jesus’ feet with costly perfume, which Jesus said was for the day of his burial (John 12:1–8). Remember. Busy service is good, but listening to Jesus comes first. Both sisters trusted him in their grief, and found him to be the resurrection and the life. Luke 10:42 but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her. Sitting at Jesus’ feet is the one thing needful. John 11:27 She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.” Martha’s great confession in her sorrow. John 12:3 Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. Lavish love for Jesus, just before his death.

Lazarus The brother of Mary and Martha of Bethany, whom Jesus raised from the dead after four days in the tomb. Who. Lazarus lived in Bethany, near Jerusalem, with his sisters Martha and Mary, and Jesus loved him as a friend (John 11:3, 11). His name is a form of Eleazar, meaning “God has helped”. Do not confuse him with the poor beggar Lazarus in Jesus’ parable of the rich man (Luke 16:19–31). Their story. When he fell ill, his sisters sent for Jesus, who waited two days so that the Son of God might be glorified (John 11:1–6). By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Jesus told Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life,” wept at the grave, and called, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man came out, still bound in grave clothes (John 11:17–44). Many believed, and the chief priests decided Jesus must die, and even planned to kill Lazarus too (John 11:45–53; 12:9–11). Remember. Lazarus was raised to die again, but his raising was a sign of Jesus’ power over death. All who believe in Christ will be raised to a life that never ends. John 11:25 Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, The promise that gives the miracle its meaning. John 11:43 When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.” Jesus’ word gives life to the dead.

Nicodemus A Pharisee and member of the Jewish council who came to Jesus by night and later helped bury him. Who. Nicodemus was a Pharisee and “a ruler of the Jews”, a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem. Jesus called him “the teacher of Israel” (John 3:10), a respected teacher of the law. He appears only in John’s Gospel. Their story. He came to Jesus by night, perhaps afraid to be seen, and called him a teacher come from God. Jesus told him that unless one is born again, or born from above, by the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God. In that talk come the famous words of John 3:16 (John 3:1–21). Later, when the council wanted to arrest Jesus, Nicodemus asked that he be given a fair hearing, and was mocked for it (John 7:45–52). After the crucifixion he came with Joseph of Arimathea, bringing about seventy-five pounds (about 34 kg) of spices to bury Jesus (John 19:38–42). Remember. Even a learned, religious man needs to be born again. Nicodemus seems to have moved from secret enquiry to open devotion, which shows that the Spirit’s work can be gradual. John 3:3 Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” New birth by God’s Spirit is needed by everyone, however religious. John 19:39 Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. The man who came by night now honours Jesus openly.

Zacchaeus A rich chief tax collector of Jericho who climbed a tree to see Jesus and was saved. Who. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, an important trading town, and he had grown rich, probably by overcharging. He was a Jew, but tax collectors were despised as cheats and collaborators with Rome. He was short. His name, ironically, comes from a Hebrew word meaning “pure” or “innocent”. Their story. When Jesus passed through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, Zacchaeus could not see over the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. Jesus stopped, called him by name, and said he must stay at his house that day. The crowd grumbled that Jesus had gone to be the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus stood and promised to give half his goods to the poor and to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated. Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:1–10). Remember. Jesus sought Zacchaeus before Zacchaeus changed. Grace came first; his generous repayment was the fruit of salvation, not its price. Luke 19:8 And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” A changed heart shows itself in changed use of money. Luke 19:10 For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Jesus’ own summary of his mission.

Joseph of Arimathea A rich member of the Jewish council, a secret disciple, who buried the body of Jesus in his own new tomb. Who. Joseph came from Arimathea, a Jewish town probably north-west of Jerusalem. He was rich (Matthew 27:57), a respected member of the council, good and righteous, and looking for the kingdom of God. He had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jewish leaders (John 19:38). Do not confuse him with Joseph of Nazareth, Mary’s husband. Their story. He had not agreed with the council’s decision to condemn Jesus (Luke 23:51). After Jesus died, he took courage and went to Pilate to ask for the body (Mark 15:43). With Nicodemus he wrapped it in linen with spices and laid it in his own new tomb cut in the rock, in a garden near the place of crucifixion, and rolled a stone across the entrance (Matthew 27:57–60; John 19:38–42). Remember. Joseph’s courage came at the darkest hour. In him Isaiah 53:9 was fulfilled: the Servant was with a rich man in his death. Luke 23:50 Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, Not every member of the council was against Jesus. Mark 15:43 Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. A secret disciple came out into the open at real risk.

Caiaphas The Jewish high priest who led the plot against Jesus and condemned him for blasphemy. Who. Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, appointed by the Romans. He was the son-in-law of Annas, the former high priest (John 18:13), and presided over the Sanhedrin (the Jewish council). He belonged to the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Acts 5:17). An ossuary (bone box) inscribed with his family name may have been found in Jerusalem in 1990. Their story. After Lazarus was raised, Caiaphas told the council it was better that one man die for the people than the whole nation perish; John says he spoke a prophecy without knowing it (John 11:47–53). He plotted with the chief priests to arrest Jesus secretly (Matthew 26:3–5). At the night trial he put Jesus under oath, and when Jesus said he was the Christ and would come on the clouds, Caiaphas tore his robes and declared it blasphemy (Matthew 26:57–66). He then sent Jesus to Pilate (John 18:28). Later he questioned Peter and John (Acts 4:5–7). Remember. Caiaphas meant evil, yet God used his words to declare the truth: Jesus died in the place of his people. John 11:50 Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish. A cynical plan that became an unknowing prophecy of substitution. Matthew 26:65 Then the high priest tore his robes and said, “He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. The high priest condemned the true High Priest.

Annas A former Jewish high priest, father-in-law of Caiaphas, to whom Jesus was first taken after his arrest. Who. Annas was high priest from AD 6 to 15, until the Romans removed him. He stayed very powerful: five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and people still called him high priest (Luke 3:2; Acts 4:6). He was a Sadducee. Their story. After the arrest in Gethsemane, Jesus was led first to Annas, who questioned him about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus replied that he had taught openly, and an officer struck him. Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas (John 18:12–24). After Pentecost, Annas was among the rulers who questioned Peter and John for preaching about Jesus (Acts 4:5–22). Remember. Annas held religious power for decades, but used it to protect his position rather than to receive God’s Messiah. Office and influence are no substitute for faith. John 18:13 First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Annas was still the power behind the high priesthood. Acts 4:6 with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. The same family that tried Jesus now opposed his apostles.

Barabbas A rebel and murderer whom Pilate released instead of Jesus at the crowd’s demand. Who. Barabbas was a prisoner in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus’ trial, about AD 30 or 33. He had taken part in an uprising against Rome and had committed murder (Mark 15:7); John calls him a robber, or bandit (John 18:40). His name means “son of the father”. Some ancient copies of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas (Matthew 27:16–17). Their story. It was the custom at Passover for the governor to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd. Pilate, believing Jesus innocent, offered to release him, but the chief priests stirred up the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead and to cry out for Jesus to be crucified. Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:6–15; Luke 23:18–25). Nothing more is known of him. Remember. Barabbas is a vivid picture of the gospel: the guilty man walked free while the innocent one died in his place. Mark 15:7 And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. He was truly guilty. Mark 15:15 So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. The great exchange, seen in one man’s release.

The Marys of the Gospels A guide to telling apart the several women named Mary in the Gospels. Who. Mary (Hebrew Miriam) was a very common name. The Gospels name at least five or six women called Mary, and it helps to know which is which. They are usually identified by a place, a husband or a son. Their story. (1) Mary the mother of Jesus, wife of Joseph (Luke 1–2). (2) Mary Magdalene, from Magdala, freed from seven demons and first witness of the resurrection (Luke 8:2; John 20). (3) Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus, who sat at Jesus’ feet and anointed him (Luke 10:39; John 12:3). (4) Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, at the cross and the tomb (Mark 15:40, 47; 16:1); Matthew calls her “the other Mary” (Matthew 28:1). (5) Mary the wife of Clopas, at the cross (John 19:25); many think she is the same as (4). Outside the Gospels there is also Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12) and a Mary greeted in Rome (Romans 16:6). The sinful woman who anointed Jesus in Luke 7 is not named and should not be identified with any of these. Remember. Several Marys stood by the cross when most of the men had fled. Their faithfulness is honoured in Scripture; each was a sinner saved by the same Lord. Mark 15:40 There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. Mark names two Marys at the cross. John 19:25 but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. John names three Marys at the cross.

Paul (Saul of Tarsus) A Pharisee who persecuted the church until the risen Jesus met him, and who became the great apostle to the Gentiles. Who. Paul was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, born in Tarsus in Cilicia and a Roman citizen from birth. Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul his Roman one. He trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel and became a strict Pharisee (Acts 22:3; Philippians 3:5). He was converted in about AD 33 to 35 and was probably executed in Rome in the mid-60s AD. He is not King Saul of the Old Testament. Their story. He approved Stephen’s stoning and hunted Christians (Acts 7:58; 8:3). On the road to Damascus the risen Jesus appeared to him, and he was baptized (Acts 9). With Barnabas, then Silas and others, he made three long journeys planting churches across Asia Minor and Greece (Acts 13–20). Arrested in Jerusalem, he appealed to Caesar and was taken to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 21–28). Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name, from Romans to Philemon. Remember. Paul never forgot that he had been a persecutor; he called himself the foremost of sinners. His life shows that grace can turn God’s fiercest enemy into his most devoted servant, and his letters set out justification by faith alone in Christ. Acts 9:15 he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. The Lord’s own words about the persecutor he had chosen. 1 Timothy 1:15 The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. Paul never stopped seeing himself as a sinner saved by grace. Galatians 2:20 I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. The heart of Paul’s life: union with Christ by faith. Paul shows that no one is too far gone for Christ to save and use.

Barnabas A generous Levite from Cyprus whose name means “son of encouragement”, and who was Paul’s first partner in mission. Who. His real name was Joseph; the apostles called him Barnabas. He was a Levite from Cyprus and an early member of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 4:36). Paul’s letters call him an apostle in the wider sense of a sent missionary, and Colossians 4:10 says John Mark was his cousin. Their story. He sold a field and gave the money to the apostles (Acts 4:37). When the disciples feared the newly converted Saul, Barnabas brought him to them (Acts 9:27). Sent to Antioch, he rejoiced at God’s grace there and fetched Saul to help him teach (Acts 11:22–26). The Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for the first missionary journey (Acts 13–14). After the Jerusalem council they parted sharply over taking Mark again, and Barnabas sailed with Mark to Cyprus (Acts 15:36–39). At Antioch he was once drawn away by Peter’s fear of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:13). Remember. Barnabas was not without faults, yet his gift was to see God’s grace in others and give them a second chance, first Saul and later Mark. That kindness reflects the God who does not give up on his people. Acts 4:36 Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, His nickname tells us what kind of man he was. Acts 11:24 for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. Luke’s warm summary of his character and the fruit of his work. Barnabas shows how much good one encourager can do in the church.

Stephen One of the seven men chosen to serve the early church, and the first Christian to die for Christ. Who. Stephen was probably a Greek-speaking Jew in the Jerusalem church. When Greek-speaking widows were being overlooked in the daily food distribution, the church chose seven men to oversee it, and Stephen was named first (Acts 6:1–6). His death came within a few years of Jesus’ resurrection, probably in the early to mid-30s AD. Their story. Full of grace and power, he did great signs among the people. Opponents could not answer his wisdom, so they brought false witnesses who said he spoke against the temple and the law (Acts 6:8–15). Before the council he traced Israel’s history and showed that the nation had always resisted God’s messengers, and had now killed the Righteous One (Acts 7:1–53). He saw heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. They dragged him out and stoned him, while a young man named Saul looked after their cloaks (Acts 7:54–60). His death scattered the church and spread the gospel (Acts 8:1–4). Remember. Stephen died like his Lord, committing his spirit to Jesus and praying for his killers. His prayer was answered in part when Saul, who watched him die, was later converted. Acts 6:8 And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. Stephen was a table servant and a powerful witness. Acts 7:59 And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” He entrusted himself to Jesus, as Jesus had entrusted himself to the Father. Acts 7:60 Lord, do not hold this sin against them. Like Christ on the cross, he prayed for those killing him. Stephen shows that dying for Christ is not defeat: the gospel spread through his death.

Philip the evangelist One of the seven chosen to serve the Jerusalem church, who preached the gospel in Samaria and to an Ethiopian official. Who. Philip was one of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the church’s widows. Later he was known as “the evangelist”, someone who travels to preach the gospel. He is not Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve (John 1:43), nor Herod Philip. He lived in Caesarea with his four unmarried daughters, who prophesied (Acts 21:8–9). Their story. When persecution scattered the church after Stephen’s death, Philip went to Samaria and proclaimed Christ, and many believed, including Simon the sorcerer (Acts 8:4–13). An angel then sent him to a desert road, where he met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53. Philip explained that the passage spoke of Jesus and baptized him (Acts 8:26–39). Afterwards he preached in the towns along the coast as far as Caesarea (Acts 8:40). About twenty years later Paul and Luke stayed at his house (Acts 21:8). Remember. Philip took the gospel beyond the Jews, first to the despised Samaritans and then to a man from distant Africa. He shows that faithful service in small tasks can lead to great opportunities, and that all Scripture points to Jesus. Acts 8:5 Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. He took the gospel to people most Jews avoided. Acts 8:35 Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. He showed the Ethiopian that Isaiah’s suffering servant is Jesus. Acts 21:8 we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. This verse tells him apart from Philip the apostle.

Silas A leader and prophet of the Jerusalem church who became Paul’s companion on his second missionary journey. Who. Silas is called Silvanus in Paul’s letters and in 1 Peter 5:12; most scholars take these to be the same man. He was a leading man in the Jerusalem church, a prophet, and, like Paul, a Roman citizen (Acts 15:22, 32; 16:37). He travelled with Paul from about AD 49 to 52. Their story. The Jerusalem council sent Silas with Judas Barsabbas to carry its letter to Antioch (Acts 15:22–32). When Paul and Barnabas parted, Paul chose Silas for his second journey (Acts 15:40). In Philippi they were beaten and jailed, yet at midnight they prayed and sang hymns; an earthquake opened the doors and the jailer and his household believed (Acts 16:19–34). He helped found the churches in Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth (Acts 17–18). He is named with Paul and Timothy in the greetings of 1 and 2 Thessalonians, and he helped Peter with his first letter (1 Peter 5:12). Remember. Silas was a faithful second man, content to serve alongside others. His songs in a prison cell show a joy in Christ that suffering could not silence. Acts 15:40 but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. Silas was chosen to share Paul’s mission. Acts 16:25 About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, Their worship in prison was itself a witness.

Timothy Paul’s young helper and “true child in the faith”, who led the church in Ephesus and received two of Paul’s letters. Who. Timothy came from Lystra, in what is now Turkey. His mother Eunice was a Jewish believer and his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). His mother and grandmother Lois taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). He joined Paul in about AD 49 and served with him for the rest of Paul’s life. Their story. Paul took him on the second journey and had him circumcised so as not to hinder the work among Jews (Acts 16:1–3). Paul sent him on hard errands to Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi (1 Thessalonians 3:2; 1 Corinthians 4:17; Philippians 2:19–22). He is named as co-sender of six of Paul’s letters. Paul left him in Ephesus to correct false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3), and from prison wrote to call him to Rome (2 Timothy 4:9). Hebrews 13:23 mentions that he was released from prison. Remember. Timothy seems to have been timid and often unwell (1 Timothy 4:12; 5:23; 2 Timothy 1:7), yet God used him greatly. His story shows the value of a godly home and of faithful teaching passed on to the next generation. 2 Timothy 1:5 a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. Timothy’s faith was nurtured by the women of his family. Philippians 2:20 For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare. Paul’s high praise for Timothy’s caring heart. Timothy encourages the young and the fearful: God’s strength is made perfect in weakness.

Titus A Greek convert and trusted helper of Paul, sent to Corinth and later left to set the churches of Crete in order. Who. Titus was a Gentile, a Greek, and Paul calls him “my true child in a common faith” (Titus 1:4), probably because Paul led him to Christ. He is never named in Acts, so we know him only from Paul’s letters. Their story. Paul took Titus with him to Jerusalem, where the leaders did not force him to be circumcised. That showed that Gentiles are saved without keeping the law of Moses (Galatians 2:1–3). Paul sent him to Corinth to deal with a troubled church and to organise the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and his good report comforted Paul greatly (2 Corinthians 7:6–7; 8:16–23). After Paul’s first Roman imprisonment, in the early 60s AD, Paul left him in Crete to appoint elders in every town, and wrote him the letter that bears his name (Titus 1:5). Later he went to Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast (2 Timothy 4:10). Remember. Titus was a living sign that the gospel is for Gentiles as well as Jews. Calm and dependable, he was a means of God’s comfort to a weary apostle. Galatians 2:3 But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Titus became a test case for salvation by grace, not by the law. 2 Corinthians 7:6 But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus, God often comforts his people through the arrival of a faithful friend.

Luke A doctor and companion of Paul who wrote the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts. Who. Paul calls him “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). He was probably a Gentile, since Paul lists him apart from his Jewish co-workers (Colossians 4:10–14). Early Christian writers agree that he wrote both Luke and Acts, which are addressed to Theophilus. He is not Lucius of Acts 13:1 or Romans 16:21, though some have suggested so. Their story. Luke did not see Jesus himself, but carefully gathered the accounts of eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). In parts of Acts he writes “we”, showing that he travelled with Paul: from Troas to Philippi, later back to Jerusalem, and finally on the voyage and shipwreck on the way to Rome (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16). He stayed with Paul in prison, and at the very end, when others had left, he was still there (2 Timothy 4:11). Remember. Luke wrote more of the New Testament than any other single writer. His Gospel shows Jesus’ care for outsiders, the poor and women, and his faithfulness to Paul shows a quiet loyalty that served Christ’s cause. Luke 1:3 it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, Luke wrote as a careful historian. 2 Timothy 4:11 Luke alone is with me. Luke stayed by Paul when others had gone. Luke shows that careful, faithful work done for Christ can bless the church for centuries.

John Mark A young man of the Jerusalem church who failed on his first mission but later became useful to Paul and wrote the Gospel of Mark. Who. His Jewish name was John and his Roman name Mark. His mother Mary had a house in Jerusalem where the church met to pray (Acts 12:12). He was a cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10). Early Christian writers say he wrote the Gospel of Mark from Peter’s preaching, and many think he was the young man who fled naked when Jesus was arrested (Mark 14:51–52). Their story. He went with Barnabas and Saul on their first journey, but turned back at Perga and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:5, 13). Paul refused to take him again, and the quarrel parted Paul and Barnabas; Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus (Acts 15:37–39). Years later Mark was with Paul in his imprisonment (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 1:24), and Peter called him “my son” (1 Peter 5:13). At the end of his life Paul asked for him because he was “very useful” (2 Timothy 4:11). Remember. Mark is the story of a second chance. One who once quit the work was restored and used to write a Gospel. Failure does not have to be final for those who belong to Christ. Acts 13:13 And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, Mark’s early failure on the first journey. 2 Timothy 4:11 Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Paul’s later verdict shows Mark had been fully restored. Mark encourages anyone who has failed in serving Christ: God restores.

James the brother of Jesus A brother of Jesus who did not believe in him at first, but became a leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote the letter of James. Who. James was one of the brothers of Jesus named in Mark 6:3. Protestants usually take these to be children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus; some traditions say cousins or Joseph’s sons from an earlier marriage. He is not James the son of Zebedee, nor James the son of Alphaeus, both among the Twelve. The Jewish historian Josephus says he was stoned in Jerusalem in about AD 62. Their story. During Jesus’ ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5). The risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and the brothers were praying with the disciples before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). He became a leading elder in Jerusalem, called a “pillar” (Galatians 2:9). Peter sent word to him after his escape from prison (Acts 12:17). At the Jerusalem council he gave the deciding judgment that Gentiles need not be circumcised (Acts 15:13–21). He is generally held to be the author of the letter of James. Remember. James grew up beside Jesus and yet did not believe until the risen Lord met him. In his letter he calls himself only “a servant” of the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace humbled and changed him. John 7:5 For not even his brothers believed in him. Even Jesus’ own family did not believe at first. 1 Corinthians 15:7 Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. The risen Christ appeared personally to his doubting brother. James 1:1 James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, He calls his own brother Lord.

Jude A brother of Jesus and of James, who wrote the short letter of Jude. Who. Jude is a form of the name Judas. He is named among Jesus’ brothers in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55. He introduces himself as “brother of James” (Jude 1:1), meaning James the leader in Jerusalem. He is not Judas Iscariot, nor the apostle Judas son of James, also called Thaddaeus (Luke 6:16). His letter was probably written in the 60s AD, though scholars differ on the date. Their story. Like his brothers, Jude did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), but after the resurrection he was among the believers praying in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14). Paul says that the Lord’s brothers travelled with their wives in Christian work (1 Corinthians 9:5). Jude wrote to warn the churches against false teachers who turned God’s grace into an excuse for immorality, and urged them to contend for the faith (Jude 1:3–4). Remember. Jude, too, came from unbelief to faith. His letter closes with one of the Bible’s greatest praises to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling. Jude 1:1 Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, He calls himself Jesus’ servant, not his brother. Jude 1:3 contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. The burden of his letter. Jude 1:24 Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, Believers are kept safe by God’s power, not their own.

Priscilla and Aquila A married couple, tentmakers by trade, who worked with Paul, taught Apollos and hosted churches in their home. Who. Aquila was a Jew from Pontus, on the Black Sea; Priscilla, also called Prisca, was his wife. They had lived in Rome until the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews, in about AD 49 (Acts 18:2). Like Paul they were tentmakers, or leatherworkers. Priscilla is often named first, perhaps because she was the more prominent in the church’s work. Their story. In Corinth Paul stayed and worked with them (Acts 18:1–3). They sailed with him to Ephesus and stayed there (Acts 18:18–19). When the gifted preacher Apollos arrived knowing only John’s baptism, they took him aside and explained the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:24–26). A church met in their house in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19), and later in Rome (Romans 16:3–5). Paul says they risked their necks for him. They were back in Ephesus when Paul wrote his last letter (2 Timothy 4:19). Remember. Priscilla and Aquila show a husband and wife serving Christ together, opening their home and gently helping others understand the gospel better. Acts 18:26 when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. They corrected Apollos privately and kindly. Romans 16:3 Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, Paul honours them as partners in his work. Romans 16:4 who risked their necks for my life, Their love for Paul cost them real danger.

Apollos An eloquent Jewish teacher from Alexandria who became a powerful preacher of Christ in Ephesus and Corinth. Who. Apollos was a Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, a great centre of learning. He was eloquent and well taught in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). He arrived in Ephesus in the early 50s AD. Some have suggested he wrote the letter to the Hebrews, but this is only a guess. Their story. He taught accurately about Jesus, but knew only the baptism of John until Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God more fully (Acts 18:25–26). He went on to Corinth, where he helped the believers greatly and showed from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ (Acts 18:27–28). Some in Corinth made him the head of a party, saying “I follow Apollos”; Paul rebuked this, insisting that he and Apollos were only servants (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6). Apollos would not return to Corinth at that time, perhaps to avoid feeding the divisions (1 Corinthians 16:12). Paul later asked Titus to help him on his way (Titus 3:13). Remember. Apollos was gifted yet teachable. His story warns against making heroes of preachers: God alone gives the growth. Acts 18:24 Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. His gifts and his knowledge of the Bible. 1 Corinthians 3:6 I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Preachers are servants; the fruit is God’s work.

Lydia A businesswoman from Thyatira whose heart the Lord opened, and who became the first known convert in Europe. Who. Lydia came from Thyatira in Asia Minor, a city famous for its dyes, and traded in costly purple cloth in Philippi in Macedonia. She was a Gentile “worshiper of God”, someone who honoured Israel’s God without becoming a Jew. She was head of her own household, so she was probably a widow or unmarried. She met Paul in about AD 49 or 50. Their story. On the Sabbath Paul and his companions went to a place of prayer by the river outside Philippi and spoke to the women gathered there. The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to Paul’s message. She and her household were baptized, and she urged the missionaries to stay in her house (Acts 16:13–15). After Paul and Silas were released from prison, they went to her house to encourage the believers before leaving the city (Acts 16:40). Her home seems to have been the first meeting place of the Philippian church. Remember. Lydia was already religious, yet she needed the Lord to open her heart. Faith is God’s gift, and her first response was generous hospitality. Acts 16:14 The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. Conversion is the Lord’s work in the heart. Acts 16:15 And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” Her new faith showed itself at once in hospitality.

Cornelius A Roman centurion in Caesarea who, with his household, became one of the first Gentiles to receive the gospel and the Holy Spirit. Who. Cornelius was a centurion, an officer commanding about a hundred soldiers, in the Italian Cohort stationed at Caesarea on the coast of Israel. He was a Gentile who feared God, gave generously to the Jewish people and prayed continually (Acts 10:1–2). These events probably took place in the late 30s AD. Their story. An angel told Cornelius to send for Simon Peter in Joppa. Meanwhile God gave Peter a vision of unclean animals and told him not to call common what God has made clean (Acts 10:3–23). Peter went to Cornelius’s house, a thing Jews normally avoided, and preached Christ. While he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard, and they were baptized (Acts 10:24–48). Peter defended this to the Jerusalem church, which praised God that he had granted repentance to the Gentiles too (Acts 11:1–18). Peter recalled it at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:7–9). Remember. Cornelius was devout and generous, yet he still needed to hear of Jesus to be saved (Acts 11:14). His story shows that God shows no partiality: the gospel is for every nation. Acts 10:2 a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. A sincere seeker, but not yet a believer in Christ. Acts 10:34 Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, Peter learned through Cornelius that the gospel is for Gentiles. Acts 10:44 While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. God himself showed he had accepted these Gentiles.

Ananias and Sapphira A married couple in the Jerusalem church who lied to God about a gift of money and died under his judgment. Who. Ananias and his wife Sapphira were members of the first church in Jerusalem, in the months after Pentecost, probably in the early 30s AD. This Ananias is not Ananias of Damascus who baptized Saul, nor the high priest Ananias (Acts 23:2). Their story. Many believers were selling property and giving the money to the apostles, and Barnabas had just done so (Acts 4:34–37). Ananias sold a piece of land but, with his wife’s knowledge, kept back part of the price while pretending to give it all. Peter said that the land and the money had been theirs to keep; their sin was to lie to the Holy Spirit. Ananias fell down and died. About three hours later Sapphira came in, told the same lie, and also died. Great fear came on the whole church (Acts 5:1–11). Remember. Their sin was not keeping some money but pretending to be more generous than they were, wanting the praise without the cost. Their story is a solemn warning that God sees the heart, and that he guards the purity of his church. Acts 5:3 why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? Peter names their sin as lying to the Holy Spirit. Acts 5:4 You have not lied to man but to God. The Holy Spirit is God; to lie to him is to lie to God. Acts 5:11 And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. God’s judgment taught the church to take him seriously. Ananias and Sapphira warn against religious show and hypocrisy.

Ananias of Damascus A devout disciple in Damascus whom the Lord sent to restore Saul’s sight and receive him as a brother. Who. Ananias was a Jewish believer in Damascus, devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews there (Acts 22:12). He lived there in the early or mid-30s AD, when Saul was converted. He is not the Ananias who lied with Sapphira, nor the high priest Ananias (Acts 23:2). Their story. The Lord spoke to Ananias in a vision and told him to go to a house on the street called Straight, where Saul of Tarsus was praying, blind. Ananias objected that Saul had done great harm to the saints and had come to arrest believers. The Lord answered that Saul was his chosen instrument (Acts 9:10–16). Ananias went, laid his hands on him and called him “Brother Saul”. Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, he regained his sight, and he was baptized (Acts 9:17–18). Paul later recalled this in his defence in Jerusalem (Acts 22:12–16). Remember. Ananias was afraid, yet he obeyed. His first words to the church’s greatest enemy were “Brother Saul”, a picture of the welcome that grace gives to those Christ has saved. Acts 9:13 Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. Ananias honestly told the Lord his fear. Acts 9:17 And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” He welcomed the former persecutor as a brother.

Dorcas (Tabitha) A disciple in Joppa, much loved for her kindness to the poor, whom God raised from the dead through Peter. Who. Tabitha is her Aramaic name and Dorcas its Greek form; both mean “gazelle”. She was a believer in Joppa, a port on the coast of Israel, and is the only woman in the New Testament specifically called a disciple. She lived in the 30s AD. Their story. She was full of good works and acts of charity. She fell ill and died, and the believers laid her body in an upper room and sent to nearby Lydda for Peter. The widows stood weeping beside him, showing him the tunics and other garments Dorcas had made for them. Peter sent everyone out, knelt and prayed, and said, “Tabitha, arise.” She opened her eyes and sat up, and he presented her alive. The news spread through Joppa and many believed in the Lord (Acts 9:36–42). Remember. Dorcas served Christ quietly, with a needle and thread, and the poor loved her for it. Her raising, like Jesus’ raising of Jairus’s daughter (Mark 5:41), shows the power of the risen Lord over death. Acts 9:36 Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. Her faith showed itself in practical love. Acts 9:39 All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. Her kindness was remembered in the clothes she had made. Acts 9:40 “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. The risen Christ gave her life again through Peter. Dorcas shows that simple, practical kindness is true service to Christ.

Philemon and Onesimus A Christian slave-owner in Colossae and his runaway slave, who became a believer through Paul; Paul’s letter to Philemon concerns them both. Who. Philemon was a believer, probably in Colossae, whom Paul had led to faith; a church met in his house (Philemon 1:1–2, 19). Onesimus, whose name means “useful”, was his slave. He had left Philemon, possibly wronging him, and somehow came to Paul in prison, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62, though scholars differ on the place. Their story. Through Paul, Onesimus became a Christian; Paul calls him “my child” (Philemon 1:10). Paul sent him back to Philemon with a short letter, and with Tychicus (Colossians 4:7–9). Paul asked Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother, to charge any debt to Paul’s account, and hinted that he might send him back to help Paul (Philemon 1:15–21). We are not told how Philemon responded. Remember. Onesimus had been useless and became useful. Paul offered to pay his debt, just as Christ took our debt on himself. In Christ, master and slave stand side by side as brothers. Philemon 1:10 I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. Onesimus was converted through Paul in prison. Philemon 1:11 (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.) Paul plays on the meaning of Onesimus’s name. Their story shows the gospel reconciling people across the deepest social divides.

Epaphras A believer from Colossae who brought the gospel to his home city and laboured for the church there in prayer. Who. Epaphras was a native of Colossae in Asia Minor (Colossians 4:12). He seems to have heard the gospel from Paul, probably during Paul’s long stay in Ephesus in the mid-50s AD, and then carried it home. Some think Epaphras is a short form of Epaphroditus, but most scholars take him to be a different man from Epaphroditus of Philippi (Philippians 2:25). Their story. He taught the Colossians the gospel and probably also served the nearby churches of Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 1:7; 4:13). Later he came to Paul in prison and reported on the church’s faith and love; it was this report, and perhaps worries about false teaching, that led Paul to write Colossians (Colossians 1:4–8). Paul calls him a faithful minister and his fellow prisoner (Philemon 1:23). Remember. Epaphras is remembered above all for prayer. Even far from home he kept struggling in prayer for his people. His example shows that prayer is real work in Christ’s service. Colossians 1:7 just as you learned it from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant. He is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf Epaphras was the one who first taught the Colossians the gospel. Colossians 4:12 always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. His love for the church showed itself in hard-working prayer.

Onesiphorus A believer from Ephesus who searched Rome to find the imprisoned Paul and was not ashamed of his chains. Who. Onesiphorus is mentioned only in 2 Timothy. He lived in Ephesus, where he had served the church in many ways (2 Timothy 1:18). He searched for Paul during Paul’s last imprisonment in Rome, in the mid-60s AD. His name means “bringer of profit”. Their story. While many in Asia had turned away from Paul, Onesiphorus came to Rome, searched hard until he found him, and often refreshed him. He was not ashamed that Paul was a prisoner in chains (2 Timothy 1:15–18). Paul asks the Lord to show mercy to his household, and at the close of the letter sends greetings to that household (2 Timothy 4:19). Some think Onesiphorus had died by then, but this is uncertain. Remember. Onesiphorus did what was costly and unglamorous: he went looking for a friend in disgrace. Christ, too, was not ashamed to call us his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). 2 Timothy 1:16 May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, Paul gave thanks for a friend who stood by him. 2 Timothy 1:17 but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me His love took real effort and courage. Onesiphorus shows the value of loyal friendship to those suffering for Christ.

Demas A co-worker of Paul who later deserted him because he loved this present world. Who. Demas is named only three times in the New Testament. He was with Paul during an imprisonment, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62, and sent greetings to the believers in Colossae and to Philemon. Nothing is known of his background. Their story. At first he was one of Paul’s “fellow workers”, named with Mark, Aristarchus and Luke (Philemon 1:24). In Colossians he is mentioned with Luke, but without any word of praise (Colossians 4:14). In Paul’s last letter, written in his final imprisonment, Paul says that Demas, in love with this present world, had deserted him and gone to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:10). We are not told whether he later returned. Remember. Demas is a sober warning that a good start in Christian service does not guarantee faithfulness to the end. The love of this world can pull even close workers away. Only God’s keeping grace holds his people firm. Philemon 1:24 and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. Demas once stood among Paul’s trusted helpers. 2 Timothy 4:10 For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. The sad end of his story as Scripture records it.

Gamaliel A respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, Paul’s old teacher, who advised the Jewish council to leave the apostles alone. Who. Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem, and was honoured by all the people (Acts 5:34). Jewish tradition calls him Gamaliel the Elder, a grandson of the famous rabbi Hillel; he died in about AD 50. Paul was taught at his feet (Acts 22:3). He is not the Gamaliel of Numbers 1:10, a leader of Manasseh. Their story. When the apostles were arrested and the council wanted to kill them, Gamaliel had them put outside. He reminded the council of earlier leaders, Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose movements had collapsed. If this movement was of man, he said, it would fail; but if it was of God, they would not be able to overthrow it, and might be found fighting against God. The council took his advice, beat the apostles and released them (Acts 5:33–40). Remember. Gamaliel’s advice was wise and cautious, and God used it to protect his apostles. Yet caution is not the same as faith. Scripture gives no sign that he believed in Jesus. Acts 5:34 But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, A man of standing and respect. Acts 5:39 but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God! His words proved true: no one could stop the gospel.

Simon the sorcerer A magician in Samaria who was baptized but tried to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit. Who. Simon practised magic in a city of Samaria and amazed the people, who called him “the power of God that is called Great” (Acts 8:9–10). He met Philip and the apostles in the mid-30s AD. Later Christian writers called him Simon Magus and made him the founder of false teaching, but Acts says nothing of this. Selling church offices came to be called “simony” after him. He is not Simon Peter or any other Simon. Their story. When Philip preached Christ in Samaria, Simon too believed, was baptized, and followed Philip, amazed at the miracles (Acts 8:12–13). When Peter and John laid hands on the Samaritan believers and they received the Holy Spirit, Simon offered them money for the same power. Peter rebuked him sharply, told him his heart was not right before God, and called him to repent. Simon asked Peter to pray for him (Acts 8:18–24). Remember. Simon’s story is a warning that outward faith and baptism are not the same as a changed heart. God’s gifts cannot be bought; they are given freely by grace. Acts 8:13 Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. His profession of faith looked real at first. Acts 8:20 May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! God’s gift cannot be bought. Acts 8:21 You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Peter saw that his heart was unchanged.

The Ethiopian eunuch A high official of the queen of Ethiopia who believed in Jesus and was baptized after Philip explained Isaiah 53 to him. Who. He was a court official in charge of all the treasure of Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians (Acts 8:27). Candace was a royal title, not a personal name. His Ethiopia was the kingdom of Cush, south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan. As a eunuch he would have been barred from the inner courts of the temple (Deuteronomy 23:1), yet he had travelled to Jerusalem to worship Israel’s God. These events took place in the mid-30s AD. Their story. On his way home he was reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot. Philip, sent by an angel, ran up and asked if he understood. He was reading Isaiah 53:7–8, about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, and asked whom the prophet meant. Beginning there, Philip told him the good news about Jesus. Coming to some water, the eunuch asked to be baptized. Then the Spirit carried Philip away, and the eunuch went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:26–39). Remember. God sought out a foreigner who could never fully belong in the temple, and welcomed him through Christ, as Isaiah had promised (Isaiah 56:3–5). Isaiah 53 is about Jesus. Acts 8:27 there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship A powerful foreign official seeking Israel’s God. Acts 8:36 See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized? Nothing now kept him out of God’s people. Acts 8:39 and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. The joy of one who has found Christ. The eunuch’s story shows the gospel reaching to the ends of the earth.
